item.title: Kaitlan Collins pulls back curtain on chaotic push to save Trump official
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened CNN’s Kaitlan Collins reported that White House officials and House Republican leaders worked “furiously” to protect Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after Republican Representative Thomas Massie reintroduced articles of impeachment on Monday. On Tuesday, the House voted 211–204 to send the articles to committee, preventing an immediate impeachment vote. According to AlterNet, Republican leaders feared absences within their own ranks could defeat that maneuver. Instead, 11 Democrats—
item.content:encoded:
What happened

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins reported that White House officials and House Republican leaders worked “furiously” to protect Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after Republican Representative Thomas Massie reintroduced articles of impeachment on Monday. On Tuesday, the House voted 211–204 to send the articles to committee, preventing an immediate impeachment vote.

According to AlterNet, Republican leaders feared absences within their own ranks could defeat that maneuver. Instead, 11 Democrats—including Nancy Pelosi—did not vote, while Massie was the only Republican to oppose sending the articles to committee. Collins said those absences may have saved Hegseth from an immediate vote, although the reporting did not establish that the Democrats intended that result.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Collins also reported that newly installed chief of staff Stephen Miller, who is personally close to Hegseth, assured him that the White House supported him. Trump publicly celebrated the outcome as Hegseth’s “exoneration,” while House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats could revive the effort after taking control in January.

Power worked behind the curtain

The decisive actors were not the television personalities narrating the scramble. They were the White House officials and House Republican leaders who used institutional power to prevent the chamber from immediately judging the impeachment articles.

Sending the measure to committee was not an acquittal. It was procedural containment. Leadership kept the question away from a direct vote, protected a Cabinet official appointed by Trump, and preserved the administration’s control over the outcome.

The alleged chaos matters less than the result. A frantic operation can still be an effective one. Republican leaders assembled enough votes to shield Hegseth, and Democratic absences supplied the margin they feared they lacked.

Absence is still agency

The 11 Democrats who did not vote should not automatically be assigned a coordinated motive the reporting does not establish. But intention and consequence are different questions. Their absence materially weakened the effort to force an immediate vote.

That distinction exposes a familiar form of congressional evasion. Members can avoid taking a recorded position while their absence changes the result just as surely as a vote would. The institution counts bodies, not private explanations.

Calling the help “unexpected” or possibly “unintentional” describes uncertainty about motive. It does not erase political responsibility for a foreseeable procedural consequence.

Trump manufactured an acquittal

Trump called the committee referral an “exoneration.” It was nothing of the kind. The House did not adjudicate the allegations described in the impeachment articles; it blocked an immediate vote by routing them elsewhere.

That rhetorical substitution is propaganda in miniature: procedural survival becomes vindication, party discipline becomes proof, and an unresolved challenge becomes partisan abuse. Trump also omitted the Democratic absences that helped produce the result because they disrupted the cleaner story he wanted to tell—total Republican loyalty defeating a purely Democratic attack.

Massie’s role further complicates that script. The effort came from a Republican, and he alone broke with his party on the decisive procedural vote. Trump answered that dissent not with an account of the underlying case, but by branding Massie a “loser.”

Controlled access, protected power

Hegseth’s Pentagon press conference reinforced the same structure. Collins said it focused largely on why he should not be impeached and that he took questions from a prepared list apparently limited to conservative outlets.

If that account is accurate, the event offered the appearance of scrutiny while management controlled who could perform it. A Cabinet official facing congressional pressure used an official platform to defend himself before a selected audience. That is message discipline masquerading as accountability.

The system protects its own

This episode reveals how executive power survives scandal or challenge: party leaders manage procedure, loyal officials reassure the threatened appointee, controlled media access narrows scrutiny, and the president relabels survival as innocence.

The central political fact is not that Washington briefly looked chaotic. It is that the governing coalition functioned precisely where it mattered. Hegseth remained protected because people with institutional authority acted to protect him—and because enough opponents failed to use the power they had.

item.title: Showdown looms as Trump staffers scramble and Dems prep blitz
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that incoming Democratic House majorities are preparing investigations into alleged self-dealing, influence peddling, politicized prosecutions, immigration abuses, and conflicts involving President Donald Trump’s administration, family, and corporate allies. Representatives Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin told administration officials to preserve records ahead of hearings expected after Democrats take control in January. The planned inquiries include reported paymen
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that incoming Democratic House majorities are preparing investigations into alleged self-dealing, influence peddling, politicized prosecutions, immigration abuses, and conflicts involving President Donald Trump’s administration, family, and corporate allies. Representatives Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin told administration officials to preserve records ahead of hearings expected after Democrats take control in January.

The planned inquiries include reported payments connected to pardons, pressure on law firms, Homeland Security contracting allegations, Elon Musk’s government role and federal contracts, the Epstein files, and the administration’s mass-deportation campaign. The article says Republican lawmakers shelved Representative Thomas Massie’s effort to begin impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, although the matter is expected to return in January.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

AlterNet also reports that administration officials are hiring lawyers while the Justice Department develops executive-privilege defenses. Attorney General Todd Blanche has threatened unspecified investigations in response, and Republicans selected Jim Jordan as minority leader, signaling an organized confrontation rather than cooperation with Democratic oversight.

The power is institutional

The decisive change is not that Democrats suddenly discovered misconduct allegations. It is that voters reportedly gave them committee gavels and subpoena power. Oversight without compulsory authority is mostly correspondence; oversight backed by Congress can force records, testimony, and public choices about whether to comply.

Trump still controls the executive branch. His administration controls departments, records, enforcement priorities, privilege claims, and the Justice Department machinery that determines whether congressional defiance carries criminal consequences. Democrats will control hearings, but the administration controls many of the doors they need opened.

That imbalance explains the scramble for lawyers. It also explains why Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff and Jim Jordan’s selection as Republican leader matter more than their combative reputations. They occupy positions from which resistance can be coordinated, normalized, and prolonged.

Resistance is a decision

Executive privilege may produce legitimate legal disputes. But privilege claims, procedural delay, refusal to produce documents, and a Justice Department unwilling to enforce subpoenas against administration allies can also function together as an obstruction system without anyone formally announcing one.

AlterNet reports that the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel has advanced a broad privilege theory covering presidential conversations with outside advisers. Courts may eventually reject or narrow it. The political value lies in the meantime: litigation can consume months or years while witnesses disperse, memories fade, and public attention moves elsewhere.

Blanche’s threat to investigate Democrats for unspecified “crimes” is more revealing still. On the facts presented, it identifies no established offense. It casts constitutionally authorized oversight as potential criminal conduct and warns investigators that exercising power may make them targets of executive power.

“Corruption” can conceal more than it clarifies

The article correctly identifies a strategic problem: using one label for every allegation can blur radically different conduct. A disputed policy choice, an undisclosed conflict, a contracting scheme, a payment for official action, and the politicized use of prosecution are not interchangeable. They demand different evidence, remedies, and degrees of culpability.

But this is not merely a messaging problem for Democrats. Treating the allegations as one atmospheric “Trump swamp” risks turning identifiable decisions into a fog of scandal. The people accused of funneling contracts, soliciting payments, trading access, or exploiting public office must be examined individually, with allegations kept distinct from proven facts.

The weaker framing would be to describe the coming conflict as partisan combat between equally situated teams. They are not equally situated. One side will be exercising congressional oversight; the other controls the executive agencies being scrutinized and, according to AlterNet, is preparing legal defenses and retaliatory investigations. Conflict is the result of those choices, not an independent actor.

Corporate power belongs inside the frame

Investigating administration officials while ignoring private beneficiaries would preserve a convenient fiction: that public corruption happens entirely inside government. The proposed scrutiny of Musk and other corporate leaders recognizes that state power can be shaped through contracts, access, technological control, and relationships that cross the public-private boundary.

AlterNet reports that Democrats want answers about Musk’s DOGE activities, his role involving satellite support for Ukraine, and the government contracts received by his companies. Those questions require evidence and careful separation of governmental authority from private business interests. They are not answered by celebrity, wealth, or proximity to the president.

Corporate actors cannot claim presidential privilege merely because they helped execute or benefited from government decisions. Following authority and money beyond the White House is therefore not an expansion of the inquiry. It is necessary to understand how the reported arrangements worked.

Accountability has to outlast Trump

Hearings can expose conduct, but exposure alone leaves the machinery intact. Democrats’ more consequential task is converting findings into rules governing presidents, Cabinet officials, judges, legislators, and contractors regardless of party.

Restrictions on stock trading, post-government compensation, contractor payments, pardon-related transactions, and conflicts of interest would move the response away from personalized scandal and toward institutional restraint. That is harder than staging confrontational hearings because durable rules can also bind the people writing them.

The systemic pattern is familiar: concentrated executive power invites private influence, partisan control suppresses scrutiny, and delayed enforcement turns legal accountability into a race against the calendar. If the incoming majority treats oversight as electoral theater, the structure survives. If it identifies decisions, beneficiaries, enabling institutions, and enforceable remedies, it can do more than document another administration’s abuses after the damage is done.

item.title: Trump’s niece singles out 'deeply corrupt' relative to be probed first
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Mary Trump urged congressional Democrats to investigate Jared Kushner, whom she called “deeply corrupt,” if the party returns to power in Congress. She criticized House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries for meeting with Kushner in August to discuss housing, immigration, and affordability, arguing that the meeting signaled a failure to take accountability seriously. Jeffries said Kushner requested the meeting and maintained that it would not prevent congression
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Mary Trump urged congressional Democrats to investigate Jared Kushner, whom she called “deeply corrupt,” if the party returns to power in Congress. She criticized House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries for meeting with Kushner in August to discuss housing, immigration, and affordability, arguing that the meeting signaled a failure to take accountability seriously.

Jeffries said Kushner requested the meeting and maintained that it would not prevent congressional investigations. Mary Trump also challenged Jeffries’ distinction between delivering economic relief and “getting even,” arguing that investigating corruption is a matter of justice with direct economic consequences—not revenge.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

She criticized Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer as well and urged voters to pressure lawmakers over leadership choices before the new Congress convenes in January. Although she predicted that both leaders would eventually support investigations, the reporting describes her demands, not any announced investigation or established finding of wrongdoing by Kushner.

Power sits with Congress

Mary Trump can command attention, but she cannot issue subpoenas, schedule hearings, or choose Democratic leaders. Jeffries and Schumer occupy the positions that matter: they influence committee priorities, legislative strategy, and whether demands for accountability become institutional action or remain partisan rhetoric.

Kushner, meanwhile, reportedly held no official government role when he met with Jeffries. That makes Jeffries’ choice politically significant. Access itself is a form of power, especially when a former presidential adviser and family member can secure a private audience with the House Democratic leader to discuss major policy questions.

Jeffries made a choice

The meeting did not simply happen. Kushner reportedly requested it, and Jeffries agreed. His assurance that conversation would not preclude investigation answers the narrow procedural concern, but not the political one Mary Trump raised: what standing did Kushner have to shape discussions about housing, immigration, and affordability?

A meeting is not proof of protection, corruption, or a bargain. But it does demonstrate that elite access survives changes in formal authority. Kushner did not need an official title to receive the attention of a party leader. Ordinary people facing unaffordable housing do not enjoy that privilege.

“Getting even” is a convenient diversion

Jeffries’ formulation turns the choice into a contest between economic work and partisan vengeance. That framing is weak. Congress can pursue affordability legislation while investigating alleged misconduct; oversight is one of its jobs, not an extracurricular indulgence.

It also shifts attention from officials’ conduct to investigators’ presumed emotions. Once accountability is labeled revenge, the central question stops being whether power was abused and becomes whether examining it looks impolite or partisan. That is how institutional caution launders inaction into statesmanship.

Mary Trump’s own call for Kushner to be jailed goes further than the reporting can support. Investigation, adjudication, and imprisonment are distinct stages, and an accusation—even a forceful one—is not a conviction. Democratic leaders should not collapse oversight into punishment, but neither should they use overheated demands as an excuse to abandon scrutiny.

Accountability and affordability are connected

Mary Trump’s strongest argument is that corruption and economic hardship are not separate subjects. Decisions about housing, immigration, taxation, contracts, and public spending determine who receives public benefits, who absorbs costs, and whose private access becomes policy influence.

That does not establish any particular allegation against Kushner. It does expose the poverty of Jeffries’ rhetorical divide. Economic relief without oversight leaves intact the channels through which connected people may influence the distribution of relief. Oversight without material action, meanwhile, becomes spectacle. A governing party should be capable of both.

The system protects access first

The larger pattern is not merely Democratic timidity or one controversial meeting. It is Washington’s durable presumption that politically connected insiders remain legitimate interlocutors even after their formal authority expires, while demands to examine their conduct are treated as potentially excessive.

Jeffries and Schumer have the institutional agency here. If they support investigations, they can help build lawful, evidence-based oversight. If they subordinate scrutiny to a performance of bipartisan normalcy, that is not confusion; it is a leadership decision with consequences. The system’s favorite form of impunity is rarely an explicit pardon. More often, it is the quiet restoration of access before accountability ever begins.

item.title: Biographer says Trump aware voters find him 'incompetent and loathsome'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that biographer Michael Wolff believes Donald Trump understood that voters increasingly regarded him as “incompetent and loathsome” after a broad political repudiation that extended into his own party. Speaking on the “Trump’s Brain” podcast, Wolff argued that Trump would answer his diminished position by intensifying his public persona rather than seeking compromise or legislative accomplishment. Wolff predicted that Trump would spend his remaining two years in of
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that biographer Michael Wolff believes Donald Trump understood that voters increasingly regarded him as “incompetent and loathsome” after a broad political repudiation that extended into his own party. Speaking on the “Trump’s Brain” podcast, Wolff argued that Trump would answer his diminished position by intensifying his public persona rather than seeking compromise or legislative accomplishment.

Wolff predicted that Trump would spend his remaining two years in office pursuing attention and projecting strength while Democrats blocked his policies and investigated allegations of corruption and self-enrichment. He also said the next president could inherit what he called Trump’s “Iran mess.” These are Wolff’s judgments and predictions; the article does not establish Trump’s private awareness independently.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Power behind the performance

The central political fact is not Wolff’s amateur diagnosis of Trump’s mind. It is that the president still held executive power. Electoral rejection, congressional resistance and personal humiliation could constrain him, but none of them converted him into a mere entertainer.

Treating Trump principally as a wounded celebrity risks confusing temperament with authority. Cameras may have supplied the validation Wolff describes, but the presidency supplied the machinery: foreign-policy discretion, administrative control and the ability to impose costs that would outlast a news cycle.

Agency does not disappear into psychology

Wolff’s account explains Trump’s anticipated conduct through narcissistic injury: a man denied admiration escalates the performance. That may be an interpretation of his incentives, but it is not an alibi.

If a president chooses spectacle over governing, retaliation over compromise or self-promotion over public responsibility, those remain political choices. Calling the struggle “an ugly battle” inside his head makes the story vivid while shifting attention away from decisions, enablers and institutional consequences.

The enabling structure

A president cannot govern through persona alone. Party officials, executive appointees and political allies decide whether grievance becomes policy and whether institutional restraints hold. Wolff’s claim that repudiation had reached Trump’s own party therefore raises the more important question: what would that party do with its remaining power?

Private disgust and electoral anxiety are not resistance. Officials who continue facilitating a president they consider diminished are exercising agency, not merely surviving his personality.

The misdirection of humiliation

The article’s framing makes public rejection sound like the engine of the coming danger. But voters who repudiated a president are weaker than the officials still positioned to restrain, investigate or enable him. Blame belongs with the people who control institutions, not with an electorate cast as the trigger for presidential rage.

The fixation on whether Trump felt loved also shrinks politics into celebrity psychology. The consequential question is not whether he could remain relevant. It is what state power could still be used for while he tried.

The systemic error

Personal rule thrives when institutions treat governance as one man’s emotional weather. The spectacle becomes the explanation, the explanation becomes an excuse, and the officials converting impulse into state action disappear from view.

Wolff’s portrait points toward a broader failure: a political system can recognize incapacity, vanity and foreseeable damage yet continue granting their bearer enormous discretion. The scandal is not simply that a president might prefer attention to accomplishment. It is that so many powerful people can understand that preference and still help make it consequential.

item.title: Scott Colom has already won
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Scott Colom had not won Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race when AlterNet published this account. He led Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,600 votes as of Monday morning, but officials in the state’s 82 counties were still reviewing eligible absentee and provisional ballots ahead of Friday’s certification deadline. Hyde-Smith had effectively declared victory on election night despite the incomplete count, then said her campaign would monitor the remaining ballots and “pr
item.content:encoded:
What happened

Scott Colom had not won Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race when AlterNet published this account. He led Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,600 votes as of Monday morning, but officials in the state’s 82 counties were still reviewing eligible absentee and provisional ballots ahead of Friday’s certification deadline.

Hyde-Smith had effectively declared victory on election night despite the incomplete count, then said her campaign would monitor the remaining ballots and “protect the integrity of the process.” Colom, who could become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since 1881, closed his campaign by invoking the sacrifice behind Black voting rights at Medgar Evers’s Jackson home.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The headline’s claim is therefore moral, not electoral: Robert Reich argues that Colom had already achieved a historic victory by making the result competitive in a state where white supremacy once excluded most Black citizens from voting through law, violence, and official complicity.

The count is the authority

The institutions with immediate power were Mississippi’s county election offices. Their officials—not either campaign, not social-media declarations, and not a columnist’s preferred historical meaning—were responsible for determining which outstanding ballots qualified and certifying the totals.

That distinction matters because democracy is not secured by declaring the right candidate symbolically victorious. It depends on administering the count accurately, allowing voters to resolve identification problems within the prescribed period, and refusing to let partisan pressure substitute for procedure.

The incumbent’s convenient posture

Hyde-Smith tried to occupy both positions available to a candidate protecting her own power: presumptive winner when the early margin appeared favorable, guardian of an unfinished process once Colom moved ahead. Her language about “integrity” did not establish misconduct. It did, however, place suspicion around ordinary ballot counting without any irregularity described in the report.

That rhetorical maneuver has a clear political use. Votes not yet counted become objects of distrust precisely when they may alter the result. Administrative procedure is recast as a threat requiring partisan vigilance. The campaign gains room to challenge an unfavorable outcome while presenting its self-interest as public protection.

History is not a substitute for power

Reich grounds Colom’s showing in Mississippi’s history of organized racial domination: Black citizens were excluded from the electorate, voting-rights workers were murdered, and state institutions declined to prosecute their killers for murder. Deputy Sheriff Cecil Ray Price did not merely belong to a hateful culture; according to the account, he used public authority to detain James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner before delivering them to fellow Klansmen.

That is the crucial lesson. White supremacy survived through institutional power—police authority, one-party control, discriminatory rules, all-white juries, and official refusal—not simply through private prejudice. The weaker framing would turn this into a sentimental story about Mississippi overcoming its past. The stronger one asks who controls the machinery now and whether every lawful ballot receives equal treatment.

Symbolism can conceal the unfinished fight

Calling Colom, Mississippi, and America winners before the count ended risks converting political struggle into national redemption. Colom’s competitiveness was historically significant. It was not the same thing as winning office, controlling a Senate seat, or ensuring that the institutions administering the election would remain insulated from partisan intimidation.

The sacrifices of Chaney, Goodman, Schwerner, Evers, and generations of Black Mississippians should not become decorative proof that the system ultimately corrects itself. The reporting itself shows otherwise: progress came because people confronted institutions built to deny them power, often while those institutions protected their attackers.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the American habit of celebrating access to power as though it were possession of power. A Black candidate approaching victory in Mississippi carries enormous historical weight, but representation becomes governing authority only after ballots are counted, results are certified, and office is won.

Colom’s campaign demonstrated what organized voters could make possible. Hyde-Smith’s shifting posture demonstrated how incumbency responds when entitlement meets uncertainty. The decisive question was not whether history had produced an inspiring symbol. It was whether Mississippi’s institutions would count lawful votes, certify the actual winner, and deny either campaign the power to turn preference into fact.

item.title: They Want to Save Small-Town America. Just Don’t Bring Any People.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: How a farmer’s proposal to revive a dying town exposed the difference between preserving a community and preserving the comfort of those already in charge. There is a peculiar American tradition of mourning the death of small towns while enthusiastically opposing almost everything that might keep them alive. Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself: ☕ Buy us a coffee The jobs are disappearing. Young people are leaving. Schools are struggling to maintain enrollment. Local busi
item.content:encoded:
How a farmer’s proposal to revive a dying town exposed the difference between preserving a community and preserving the comfort of those already in charge.

There is a peculiar American tradition of mourning the death of small towns while enthusiastically opposing almost everything that might keep them alive.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The jobs are disappearing. Young people are leaving. Schools are struggling to maintain enrollment. Local businesses are closing. Family farms are becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.

And everyone agrees that something must be done.

Until someone proposes actually doing something.

Then, suddenly, there are concerns.

About traffic. About noise. About development. About housing. About preserving the community’s unique character.

Apparently, the most important characteristic of a small American town is that it must remain small — even if that eventually means nobody lives there.

Farmer and agricultural entrepreneur Chris Newman recently offered a particularly infuriating illustration of this contradiction.

And unlike the usual abstract arguments about rural decline, his story comes with an actual building, an actual development proposal, and an actual community where much of the surrounding context can be independently corroborated.

The story is ridiculous.

But the political machinery behind it is anything but funny.

A Building, a Plan, and a Future

Chris Newman is not some random internet personality offering unsolicited advice about farming.

He is a founder of Sylvanaqua Farms and a co-founder of Blackbird Farms, a cooperative agricultural enterprise in Virginia. His work has focused on making farming economically viable by sharing infrastructure, coordinating production, and connecting agricultural operations with processing and distribution.

In other words, he has spent years working on the very problem rural politicians routinely claim to be desperate to solve.

In a video titled “They Know How to Save Rural Communities. They Just Won’t Do It,” Newman describes a former Coca-Cola bottling plant in the center of his town.

The building, he says, had been sitting unused for years.

He had a plan. He had an investor.

And his proposal went considerably beyond opening another boutique store selling overpriced candles to tourists.

He wanted to transform the property into a functioning agricultural and commercial hub.

The centerpiece would be a small-scale poultry processing facility. The building would also contain a butcher shop, a bakery, affordable housing, and classrooms to train new farmers.

Those farmers would supply the processing operation, creating a local agricultural supply chain.

According to Newman, the proposed development would have generated more than two dozen year-round jobs, millions in annual retail revenue, and opportunities for younger people to establish permanent livelihoods in the community.

It also aimed to preserve surrounding farmland by keeping it economically productive.

Consider what that means.

Jobs. Housing. Education. Local manufacturing. Food production. Tax revenue. Agricultural preservation.

Not a speculative cryptocurrency mining facility. Not another chain store sending its profits to a distant corporate headquarters.

An integrated local economy, designed to keep money, workers, and productive capacity in the community.

The sort of proposal that economic-development officials usually spend years trying to attract.

And then came the local government.

The Horror of Having a Functioning Town

According to Newman, the redevelopment required local land-use approval.

When he presented his proposal, officials reportedly appreciated the butcher shop, the bakery, and the restaurant component.

But they had reservations about the jobs and housing.

Why?

Because those elements would conflict with the “small-town character” envisioned in the community’s master plan.

Read that again.

The jobs and housing were the problem.

Not some potentially hazardous industrial operation. Not an enormous warehouse complex generating hundreds of daily truck movements.

The very things needed to attract and retain residents were allegedly incompatible with the town’s desired identity.

There is something almost impressively absurd about wanting a bakery but objecting to the economic development that would give people the means to work there, buy bread there, and live nearby.

It's the municipal equivalent of ordering a restaurant meal and then complaining that someone had the audacity to build a kitchen.

Of course, there can be legitimate objections to a particular development. Poultry processing requires environmental safeguards. Mixed-use conversions raise questions about wastewater, traffic, building codes, and permitted land uses.

Those are real issues. They deserve real scrutiny.

But “we like the commercial amenities, just not the jobs and housing” is not a serious economic-development strategy.

It's a wish list for a town that wants all the benefits of civilization without the inconvenience of other people participating in it.

We Checked. This Is a Real Place.

Newman's story points toward Montross, Virginia, a small community in Westmoreland County.

The historical record confirms that Montross has a former Northern Neck Coca-Cola bottling plant at 15725 Kings Highway. The brick facility opened in 1932 and became part of the town's commercial and industrial identity.

The Virginia Department of Historic Resources documents its history, including the expansion of the operation over subsequent decades.

The documentary record does not independently establish that this was the exact building in Newman's proposal, and it suggests a shorter period of disuse than his description of roughly thirty years. But the physical and historical setting he describes is real.

More importantly, the town and surrounding county have formal planning frameworks addressing development, historic preservation, and community character.

And here is where the story becomes especially interesting.

Montross has already undertaken an official downtown revitalization initiative.

According to the Northern Neck Planning District Commission, the initiative began in 2007, received state community-development funding in 2013, and was completed in 2015.

It included facade improvements, landscaping, streetlights, benches, signs, pedestrian crossings, and murals.

The project also included a revolving-loan fund intended to support job creation.

More than a million dollars in combined public and private investment went into improving the downtown.

None of that is inherently bad. Public spaces matter. Historic preservation matters. Making a town attractive to residents and visitors matters.

But there is a revealing distinction between making a town look prosperous and creating the conditions that allow people to prosper.

A mural doesn't pay a mortgage.

A decorative streetlight doesn't create a career.

And a freshly painted storefront doesn't solve the problem of young families being unable to afford a home.

If Newman's description of the officials' response is accurate, we have a remarkable contrast: a town publicly committed to revitalization, but officials allegedly reluctant to accommodate the jobs and housing associated with a particular revitalization proposal.

We have not independently verified the officials' conversation or a formal rejection of his plan. That remains Newman's firsthand account.

But the broader contradiction deserves scrutiny regardless.

What exactly are we revitalizing if we aren't making room for people to build lives there?

The Town Is Not a Museum

This brings us to the central problem with the phrase “small-town character.”

It sounds wonderfully wholesome.

It evokes historic buildings, friendly neighbors, quiet streets, familiar businesses, and communities where people know one another.

And there is nothing wrong with valuing those things.

But sometimes the phrase stops describing what makes a community special and starts functioning as a political weapon against anything that might change it.

A town is not a museum exhibit.

Its residents are not historical reenactors.

And its purpose is not to preserve a particular generation's preferred level of traffic indefinitely.

A living community necessarily changes.

Children grow up. Families move in. Businesses open and close. Industries evolve. Buildings acquire new purposes.

The community that existed fifty years ago was itself the product of changes that earlier generations accepted, encouraged, or fought over.

Montross's own historic Coca-Cola plant illustrates the point beautifully.

In 1932, somebody built an industrial operation that became part of the town's economic history.

Today, that building is recognized as part of its historic fabric.

Imagine if the officials of 1932 had decided that a bottling plant would disturb the quaint character of their community.

What exactly would future generations have been preserving?

Yesterday's development becomes today's heritage.

But only if yesterday's leaders allow it to happen.

Preservation becomes destructive when it stops protecting a community's identity and starts preventing that community from developing a future.

The Comfortable Politics of Decline

Newman goes further than criticizing zoning decisions.

He argues that some of the older officials governing sparsely populated communities don't actually want those communities to thrive.

What they want, he suggests, is quiet.

No traffic. No parking problems. No crowded restaurants. No noisy children. No competition for local services.

Just enough economic activity to maintain the amenities they already enjoy.

It's a harsh characterization, and it would be unfair to assume every older resident or local official thinks this way.

Age is not the problem.

Political power insulated from the consequences of its own decisions is the problem.

Consider the incentives.

An established homeowner may have paid off their mortgage decades ago.

They may be retired, with no need to find local employment.

Their children may already have moved away.

Their property may be increasing in value precisely because housing supply is constrained.

For that person, additional housing, industry, and population growth may appear to offer relatively little personal benefit.

But the young adult trying to remain in the community faces an entirely different calculation.

Where are the jobs?

Where are the affordable homes?

Where is the economic ladder that allows someone to start as an employee and eventually support a family?

If the town's answer is essentially “somewhere else,” then people will go somewhere else.

And when they leave, the remaining residents can lament the disappearance of the next generation.

The cruelty of this arrangement doesn't require every participant to consciously desire the outcome.

It requires only that the people benefiting from the status quo have enough power to preserve it, while the people who need change have too little power to demand it.

In fact, those younger people may not even live within the jurisdiction anymore.

They have already been pushed out.

Their absence then becomes politically convenient.

Second Homes Are Not a Substitute for Neighbors

Newman identifies another mechanism worth examining.

If permanent residents are inconvenient, wealthy outsiders buying second homes can appear to offer an attractive alternative.

They purchase property.

They pay property taxes.

They may spend money locally when they visit.

And, crucially, they aren't around all the time.

For communities prioritizing property values and low population density, that can seem like an excellent arrangement.

But a second home is not the same thing as a year-round household.

An occasional resident doesn't provide the same consistent demand for groceries, childcare, local services, schools, or everyday commerce.

A town can accumulate valuable real estate without developing a correspondingly robust local economy.

Worse, demand from wealthier outside buyers can push property prices beyond the reach of the people who work in the community.

The teacher, the mechanic, the restaurant employee, and the agricultural worker become increasingly unable to afford the place their labor helps sustain.

And eventually the town discovers a strange problem.

It has attractive houses.

It has charming storefronts.

It has historic character.

It just doesn't have enough people who can afford to live and work there.

That isn't necessarily revitalization.

It can be gentrification without the inconvenience of urban density.

Or, put less politely, turning an actual community into a retirement-and-vacation product.

The Government Isn't Always Somewhere Else

There is an additional layer of hypocrisy in the politics of rural economic decline.

American political discourse frequently treats rural communities as helpless victims of distant forces.

Washington forgot them.

Corporate America abandoned them.

Globalization destroyed their industries.

And there is plenty of evidence that national policy, economic consolidation, and corporate decisions have damaged rural economies.

But local government is not merely a passive spectator.

Zoning boards, planning commissions, town councils, and county supervisors wield enormous influence over what can be built, where people can live, and which businesses are allowed to operate.

A politician can spend every election cycle demanding that someone bring jobs back.

Then return home and oppose the housing needed for those workers.

A town can spend public money promoting economic development.

Then reject proposals because development might actually change something.

This is why examining local government matters.

It's easy to blame distant institutions.

It's considerably less comfortable to discover that the people obstructing economic opportunities may be the same people sitting at the next town council meeting.

And the underlying issue is not unique to rural America.

Suburban communities routinely fight new housing while complaining that their adult children cannot afford to live nearby.

Affluent neighborhoods oppose apartments while lamenting homelessness.

Municipalities demand thriving commercial districts while restricting the residential density necessary to support them.

The details change.

The contradiction remains.

We want the benefits of a functioning society, but we reserve the right to veto the arrangements that make it function.

Stop Calling It Revitalization If You Oppose Life

None of this means every development proposal deserves approval.

Newman's plan was ambitious. It would have needed to satisfy legitimate regulatory, environmental, financial, and operational requirements.

An attractive business model is not an automatic entitlement to a zoning change.

But there is a world of difference between requiring a developer to address concrete problems and declaring that jobs and permanent housing are fundamentally incompatible with the character of a town.

The first is governance.

The second is an ideological preference masquerading as planning.

And when that preference is exercised by people who already possess the homes, security, and community amenities denied to younger generations, it becomes a particularly ugly form of gatekeeping.

We should also reject the lazy temptation to turn this into a generational morality play.

Not every boomer opposes development. Not every younger person supports it. There are retirees who fight for affordable housing and younger property owners who fight just as fiercely against it.

The relevant division is between those willing to accommodate a community's future and those determined to freeze it around their own interests.

Newman's experience matters because it exposes how that conflict can play out in an actual place, with an actual entrepreneur attempting to create something tangible.

It also exposes the emptiness of a political vocabulary that celebrates economic development while treating the basic ingredients of economic development as threats.

Jobs require workers.

Workers require housing.

Businesses require customers.

Families require stability.

Agriculture requires infrastructure, markets, and people who can earn a living doing the work.

These are not radical propositions.

They are the operating requirements of a functioning community.

A town that refuses to accommodate them cannot reasonably expect its population and economy to flourish through nostalgia alone.

The Future Is Supposed to Outlive You

There is something profoundly selfish about treating a community's future as an inconvenience to its present residents.

A town is not the personal property of whichever generation happens to hold political power.

It is an inheritance from people who built before us and an obligation to people who will live after us.

Every road, storefront, farm, school, workshop, and neighborhood exists because someone, at some point, accepted that the community needed to grow or change.

The people who benefit from those decisions today have no special moral entitlement to deny comparable opportunities to those who come next.

Chris Newman's account is infuriating precisely because the solution he describes wasn't mysterious.

He wasn't demanding that someone invent a new industry, reverse globalization, or persuade millions of young people to move to the countryside.

He was proposing to use an existing building to create jobs, housing, training, and productive local businesses.

And according to him, the political objection was that too much of that activity would disrupt the community's character.

Maybe those officials sincerely believed they were protecting their town.

Maybe they had legitimate concerns that weren't adequately addressed.

Or maybe Newman correctly identified a governing class more interested in its own tranquility than in the community's long-term survival.

Whatever their motives, the principle remains:

You cannot preserve a living community by systematically excluding the things that keep it alive.

If your vision of small-town America has room for historic buildings but not new workers, room for tourist attractions but not affordable homes, room for nostalgic storefronts but not the families who would sustain them, then you aren't really saving a town.

You're preserving the scenery.

And when the last young family leaves, the last school closes, and the last local business loses its customers, the scenery will still be there.

Quiet.

Beautiful.

And utterly lifeless.

Congratulations. You preserved the character.

You just killed the town.

Sources and further reading

  • Chris Newman, Blackbird Coop / Farming While Beige, “They Know How to Save Rural Communities. They Just Won’t Do It”. Primary firsthand account.

  • Blackbird Farms — About the Founders. Background on Newman and the agricultural cooperative.

  • Jacqui Shine, “Chris Newman Wants to Help You Start Farming—Without Ruining Your Life,” Modern Farmer, March 28, 2024.

  • Virginia Department of Historic Resources — Montross Historic District. Historical documentation of the Northern Neck Coca-Cola bottling plant.

  • Northern Neck Planning District Commission — Montross Revitalization. Documentation of the town's 2007–2015 revitalization initiative.

  • Town of Montross — Zoning and Community Development. The municipality's published development-planning framework.

  • Westmoreland County Comprehensive Plan: Vision 2030. County-level planning context, distinct from the municipality's own zoning authority.

item.content:encoded:
How billionaires turn stocks into spending money, tax deductions, and political influence — while insisting their fortunes aren't taxable income.

There is a peculiar creature in American economics: the billionaire who is simultaneously too poor to pay taxes and wealthy enough to purchase almost anything.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Ask how much money this person has, and the answer is billions. Ask how much income they have, and suddenly the conversation becomes complicated.

“That’s not income,” we're told. “It's unrealized appreciation. They don't actually have that money.”

Fair enough.

Except when they want to buy a yacht.

Or another mansion.

Or an entire company.

Then, miraculously, those supposedly inaccessible billions become useful again.

And when the billionaire decides to donate some of that wealth to charity, the tax system performs yet another remarkable transformation: assets that supposedly weren't income can suddenly support a charitable deduction based on their market value.

Welcome to the wonderful world of American billionaire taxation, where wealth is real when it provides purchasing power, unrealized when taxation comes knocking, and charitable when it generates favorable publicity.

The contradictions are not necessarily evidence of illegal behavior.

They're features of the system.

The Billionaire Who Doesn't Need a Paycheck

Most Americans understand taxation through a relatively straightforward process.

You work. You earn money. The government takes its share.

Your employer doesn't generally give you the option of declaring that your paycheck represents unrealized potential and therefore shouldn't be taxed.

Billionaires, however, often accumulate their fortunes differently.

Consider someone who owns $10 billion in company stock. Those shares appreciate to $15 billion. Their net worth increases by $5 billion, but under the ordinary American income-tax rules, that appreciation generally isn't taxable until the shares are sold.

There are legitimate economic and administrative reasons for distinguishing unrealized gains from realized income. Markets fluctuate. Valuations can change. Selling assets to meet a tax obligation can create liquidity problems.

But something interesting happens when we introduce borrowing.

Our billionaire approaches a financial institution and offers a portion of that appreciated stock as collateral for a loan.

The bank evaluates the shares, accepts the collateral, and provides hundreds of millions of dollars in cash.

The billionaire can now spend that money.

The transaction generally doesn't trigger income tax because borrowed money creates an obligation to repay. A loan isn't ordinarily income.

And that distinction makes perfect sense in isolation.

What becomes controversial is the arrangement that emerges when someone possesses enough appreciating assets to borrow repeatedly, finance an extravagant lifestyle, and avoid selling substantial holdings.

The arrangement has a name.

Buy, Borrow, Die.

Buy appreciating assets. Borrow against them instead of selling. Eventually die, leaving heirs who may benefit from a step-up in the assets' tax basis.

Under existing rules, that final step can eliminate federal income tax on substantial appreciation that occurred during the deceased owner's lifetime.

The underlying wealth was genuine enough to secure loans.

The borrowed cash was genuine enough to purchase luxury goods.

But the appreciation itself may never have appeared as taxable capital gains.

It's a remarkably convenient distinction.

The Liquidity Paradox

Whenever someone proposes taxing billionaires based on their enormous holdings, a familiar defense appears.

“They don't have billions sitting in a checking account!”

Of course they don't.

Nobody seriously imagines that Jeff Bezos keeps his fortune in a gigantic savings account, occasionally walking into a bank branch to withdraw enough money to purchase a cruise ship.

The argument deliberately confuses liquidity with economic capacity.

An individual who owns $20 billion in readily tradable securities is not economically equivalent to someone with $20 in their wallet merely because neither has sold those securities today.

Banks understand this perfectly.

They routinely evaluate assets as collateral. They recognize that stocks have economic value even before their owners sell them.

The tax system recognizes this value, too, in numerous contexts.

And that gives us a useful principle:

If an asset's value is sufficiently real to support hundreds of millions in personal borrowing, policymakers can reasonably examine whether using that value should trigger some recognition of previously untaxed appreciation.

This doesn't require declaring every loan taxable income.

A family borrowing against its home to repair the roof isn't the same economic situation as a billionaire borrowing hundreds of millions against a massive stock portfolio to finance personal spending.

A sensible policy can distinguish between the two.

The objection that billionaires “don't have the money” cannot, by itself, settle the taxation question when financial institutions are already willing to provide that money against their assets.

Enter the Philanthropist

Now comes the second act.

Comedian Alex Falcone recently examined billionaire philanthropy in a video asking whether the entire enterprise might be a scam.

His presentation is deliberately humorous, but it raises questions that extend well beyond individual billionaires behaving badly.

Consider what happens when our hypothetical billionaire decides to donate $100 million in highly appreciated stock.

If the shares meet the applicable requirements, the billionaire can transfer them directly to a qualified charitable organization without first selling them and realizing the appreciation.

Depending on the recipient, the type of stock, and the applicable limitations, the donor may also qualify for a charitable deduction based on the shares' fair market value.

Let that sink in.

When the billionaire wants to spend against the assets, they're valuable collateral.

When the government considers taxing their appreciation, the gains haven't been realized.

And when the billionaire wants a charitable deduction, the donated shares have a recognized market value.

Legally, these are different transactions, governed by different provisions of the tax code. The distinctions aren't imaginary, and the tax deduction isn't automatically equal to the donation's value.

But together they reveal something important: the same financial wealth receives remarkably different treatment depending on what its owner decides to do with it.

And the story gets considerably more interesting when the charitable recipient isn't an independent organization delivering immediate assistance.

What happens when the billionaire gives the money to a foundation associated with the billionaire?

The Charity That Keeps the Money

Private foundations can perform important charitable work. They finance medical research, education, disaster relief, scientific programs, and countless other activities.

Their legal structure also allows assets to remain invested while charitable spending is distributed over time.

Most U.S. private nonoperating foundations are subject to an annual minimum-distribution regime, generally calculated around 5% of relevant investment assets, with adjustments and qualifying expenses.

That matters because it means the commonly repeated claim that foundations have no obligation to spend anything is inaccurate.

But it also means a foundation can ordinarily preserve a substantial portion of its assets in any given year.

Imagine donating $1 billion to a foundation you establish.

You no longer personally own that money. The foundation is legally separate, subject to charitable-purpose requirements and restrictions on self-dealing.

Those restrictions are important.

Nevertheless, the donor and associates may continue to exercise considerable influence over the foundation's priorities through its governance.

The money can remain invested, potentially generating returns, while the foundation distributes qualifying amounts over time.

The donor receives recognition for a billion-dollar charitable commitment even though the benefits to operating charities or intended beneficiaries may emerge over many years.

This isn't necessarily fraudulent.

It's an entirely different arrangement from handing a billion dollars directly to organizations serving people today.

And American public discourse routinely treats the two as interchangeable.

The billionaire gets the headlines now.

Society may receive the benefits later.

Philanthropy Without the Philanthropist's Name

There is another charitable mechanism worth examining: the donor-advised fund.

A donor-advised fund, or DAF, allows someone to contribute assets to a sponsoring charitable organization while retaining advisory privileges concerning future distributions and investments.

The sponsor legally controls the donated assets. The donor generally cannot simply reclaim them for personal use.

Yet the donor can receive an eligible tax deduction when making the contribution, even if the assets don't immediately reach an operating charity.

Unlike private nonoperating foundations, individual donor-advised fund accounts generally aren't subject to a comparable annual payout requirement.

And donor-advised funds can provide an additional benefit: privacy.

The ultimate recipients of charitable grants may receive money from the sponsoring organization without the original donor necessarily being publicly identified.

Privacy isn't inherently sinister. Some donors have entirely legitimate reasons for avoiding publicity.

But donor anonymity also complicates efforts to understand who finances organizations engaged in political, ideological, or controversial social campaigns.

The public may learn that a charitable organization received funding without knowing which extraordinarily wealthy individual originally supplied it.

Once again, the question is not whether every such donation is abusive.

The question is whether the public receives sufficient accountability in exchange for the substantial tax advantages offered to donors.

If the public treasury effectively subsidizes charitable giving through forgone tax revenue, should the public have no meaningful way to understand the concentration of influence behind that giving?

When Charity Meets Business

Falcone's video offers a particularly revealing example involving Elon Musk.

An October 2026 investigation by Mississippi Today documented millions of dollars donated to the Southaven Police Department by Musk-associated business interests and the Musk Foundation.

According to the reporting, the Musk Foundation provided $1.85 million for police equipment, including Flock surveillance cameras and an autonomous drone system.

The donations occurred amid the development of a nearby data-center project associated with Musk's businesses.

Local officials characterized the foundation's contribution as a public-safety grant, and the reporting described a separate business donation agreement explicitly disclaiming any exchange of benefits.

Those details matter. The available reporting does not establish that the foundation purchased government approval.

But it does establish a relationship worth examining.

A billionaire's private business interests and charitable activities operated in the same community, around the same time, as local officials were dealing with the consequences of a major industrial development.

And some of the philanthropic resources supported expanded police surveillance capabilities.

Consider the questions this raises.

Who determines what constitutes a public benefit?

Who decides whether more surveillance equipment is preferable to additional teachers, expanded healthcare, or infrastructure improvements?

Should private philanthropic funding be allowed to reshape local public-service priorities without the level of democratic deliberation normally associated with public spending?

The billionaire may regard the donation as generous.

City officials may appreciate resources that their budgets otherwise couldn't provide.

Residents, however, still live with the consequences of the decisions made.

A charitable donation does not automatically answer whether the funded project serves their interests.

And the existence of a tax advantage makes that question more—not less—important.

When Generosity Becomes Governance

Here is the issue that too often disappears beneath the celebration of billionaire philanthropy.

Tax deductions are not free.

When the government allows a taxpayer to reduce taxable income through qualifying charitable contributions, it generally forgoes revenue it otherwise might have collected.

That does not mean every donated dollar would otherwise have become a dollar of tax revenue. Deduction values depend on rates, limits, and individual circumstances.

It does mean charitable deductions represent a public policy choice.

Society has decided to encourage particular activities through favorable tax treatment.

The resulting private charitable spending can provide genuine benefits.

But it also gives donors substantial discretion over which purposes receive support.

And the wealthier the donor, the more consequential that discretion can become.

An ordinary worker generally cannot redirect their federal tax liability into a personally selected charitable initiative.

A billionaire can sometimes make an enormous qualifying donation, reduce their tax bill, and continue influencing how the charitable assets are deployed.

The two individuals aren't exercising comparable economic power.

Wealth already translates into influence over corporations, markets, media, and politics.

Charitable structures can add another channel through which private wealth shapes public life.

This raises an uncomfortable democratic question:

When public policy subsidizes private philanthropy, how much public influence should one extremely wealthy individual be allowed to purchase with the resulting tax advantages?

Not every dollar of philanthropic influence is improper. Not every charitable foundation is a vanity project. And publicly funded programs are hardly immune to waste, corruption, or misguided priorities.

But pointing out government imperfections doesn't eliminate the accountability problem.

The billionaire's personal preferences are not automatically a substitute for democratic decision-making.

A Tax System That Recognizes Economic Reality

The obvious response is not to declare all philanthropy fraudulent, outlaw borrowing, or tax every fluctuating dollar of paper wealth as though it were cash.

The challenge is to design rules that recognize how substantial wealth actually functions.

Consider several reforms.

First, address borrowing against enormous appreciated holdings.

For ultrawealthy taxpayers, substantial personal borrowing secured by appreciated financial assets could trigger a narrowly defined tax event or a prepayment against future capital-gains liability.

The system would need thresholds, exclusions, protections against double taxation, and rules distinguishing ordinary financing from arrangements primarily used to access untaxed appreciation.

The purpose would not be to tax the entire borrowed amount as though it were wages.

It would be to prevent indefinite borrowing from functioning as a permanent substitute for realizing taxable gains.

Second, reconsider the step-up in basis at death.

Under current rules, inherited assets often receive a new tax basis reflecting their value at the owner's death.

That can erase federal income tax on appreciation accumulated over decades.

Congress could instead require recognition of gains at death, carry over the original basis, or adopt a hybrid system with exemptions and deferrals for genuinely illiquid family businesses and other appropriate circumstances.

There is no compelling economic reason to assume that appreciation disappears merely because its owner does.

Third, distinguish charitable giving from charitable warehousing.

If a donor receives significant tax benefits immediately, the charitable structure should provide meaningful assurance that those assets will serve qualifying public purposes within a reasonable period.

This is especially relevant to donor-advised funds, where an individual account can lack a statutory annual distribution requirement.

Reforms could introduce payout deadlines, stronger disclosure rules, or different tax treatment depending on when assets actually reach charitable programs.

Fourth, scrutinize transactions where philanthropic spending and private business interests overlap.

Not every such transaction is improper.

But when a billionaire's charitable organization funds projects in communities where the billionaire's businesses seek approvals, infrastructure, or other advantages, stronger transparency can help establish whether public benefits are being independently evaluated.

Charity should not become an opaque substitute for corporate expenditures or public accountability.

The Question Isn't Whether Billionaires Give

Some billionaires contribute significant resources to causes that genuinely improve people's lives.

That deserves acknowledgment.

A medical breakthrough financed by philanthropic donations remains valuable regardless of the donor's tax bracket.

A child receiving treatment doesn't become less healthy because the funding came from a wealthy person's foundation.

The benefits are real.

But useful philanthropy does not automatically justify every tax preference surrounding it.

Nor should society treat charitable donations as compensation for weaknesses elsewhere in the tax system.

A billionaire can fund a hospital and still be subject to legitimate questions about how their wealth is taxed.

A foundation can do important work while still exercising disproportionate influence over public priorities.

And someone who gives away millions can remain a beneficiary of arrangements that allow enormous appreciation to escape income taxation.

These propositions aren't mutually exclusive.

Philanthropy and taxation serve different purposes.

One allows individuals to support causes they choose.

The other finances collectively determined obligations.

A functioning society needs room for both.

What it doesn't need is a system that allows private charitable activity to become a rhetorical shield against scrutiny of how enormous fortunes accumulate, finance consumption, and transfer across generations.

The Money Was Always Real

Return to our supposedly cash-poor billionaire.

They own billions in stock.

They borrow against it to finance personal expenditures.

They transfer some of it into a charitable structure and potentially receive substantial tax benefits.

They retain influence over the distribution of donated assets, subject to the applicable legal restrictions.

And when the conversation turns to taxing their vast appreciation, we're reminded that the wealth isn't really income.

There is a legitimate legal distinction between owning appreciated property and realizing taxable gains.

But a legal distinction is not a commandment carved into stone.

Tax law is a set of policy choices. Those choices can be evaluated against economic reality, changed when they produce undesirable incentives, and redesigned when they no longer serve their stated purposes.

The debate shouldn't be reduced to whether billionaires have enormous piles of cash sitting in bank accounts.

Their economic power doesn't depend on that.

Their borrowing capacity demonstrates it.

Their philanthropic commitments demonstrate it.

Their ability to influence entire industries and communities demonstrates it.

The real question is whether the tax system should continue allowing that economic power to generate substantial private benefits while portions of the underlying appreciation remain untaxed indefinitely.

If wealth is real enough to borrow against, real enough to buy companies with, and real enough to generate charitable tax deductions, it is real enough to be considered when designing a fair tax system.

The money was never imaginary.

Only the insistence that it couldn't possibly be taxed was.

item.title: Buckle up for the most dangerous 8 weeks in American history
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet's commentary warns that the weeks before newly elected Democrats take their seats could bring escalating executive retaliation. Political-violence researcher Robert Pape supplies its central eight-week warning, while historian Ruth Ben-Ghiat describes the danger of a weakened authoritarian leader consolidating loyalists and attacking opponents.

The piece connects that warning to Trump's appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff, his demand that Democratic members of Congress be imprisoned, and Todd Blanche's comments about possible investigations of lawmakers. Asked by CNN about pursuing Democrats, Blanche said the answer depended on what they had said or done and whether a crime was involved. The article anticipates a January transfer of congressional power while describing an executive branch that retains the machinery to retaliate in the meantime.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The power sits inside institutions

A president's anger acquires consequences through the people and institutions that act on it. An investigative demand needs officials willing to translate it into assignments, inquiries, and pressure. The consequential question is how the Justice Department and other agencies exercise the discretion they possess.

AlterNet describes the financial damage an investigation can inflict even before any case reaches a courtroom. That mechanism matters. A political opponent can spend resources answering scrutiny while the institution directing it draws on public authority and public money. The imbalance exists throughout the process, including when the ultimate allegation fails.

Blanche's reference to possible crimes preserves an important qualification in what he said. The political concern comes from its setting: the president was demanding imprisonment for opponents while his acting attorney general entertained investigative possibilities. Officials can turn that combination into a signal that criticism invites institutional attention.

Miller's promotion concentrates responsibility

The article presents Miller's appointment as an escalation, citing reporting about his involvement in domestic deployments, efforts to restrict mail-in voting, and the administration's treatment of political adversaries. Those reported actions give the appointment institutional significance beyond the temperament of the person receiving it.

Trump made the appointment. Describing him as wounded, enraged, or weakened can obscure that continuing agency. He retains the power to select senior officials and define the conduct his administration rewards. Elevating a loyalist associated with aggressive uses of executive authority communicates a governing preference to everyone beneath him.

The same accountability reaches the officials who implement that preference. Personal loyalty can become an administrative incentive: anticipate what the president wants, demonstrate usefulness, and treat institutional limits as obstacles to advancement. Each participant still makes a decision about what to authorize, pursue, or resist.

The warning is about a mechanism

An eight-week danger window expresses an assessment of risk. Its political value depends on identifying the decisions through which escalation could occur. Treating the most catastrophic possibilities as inevitable would obscure the choices and constraints that still determine events.

The article's concrete concern is executive retaliation before congressional oversight changes hands. Trump can make demands; agency leaders and subordinates decide how those demands enter government practice. An election result changes the political environment while leaving those existing powers available during the transition.

That is why a weakened leader can remain consequential. Electoral losses can increase the incentive to protect allies, intimidate investigators, or obstruct accountability. The incentive alone establishes no particular future act. It identifies a conflict between an officeholder's personal interests and the public responsibilities of the institutions he directs.

An election does not administer its own result

AlterNet also describes the oversight powers incoming Democratic legislators may exercise. Those powers create a prospective check on executive conduct, subject to the decisions and institutional conditions through which Congress actually uses them.

The larger issue is how government behaves between electoral judgment and its institutional consequences. A president's capacity to cause harm during that interval depends on the officials who convert his preferences into action and the constraints they honor.

When public institutions treat the leader's grievances as their operating instructions, personal retaliation gains administrative reach. When officials preserve limits on their own discretion, the same machinery can contain that reach. The transition is therefore a continuing contest over who government serves, conducted through identifiable choices by people who hold public power.

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Judge Ana Reyes ordered federal agencies to preserve records related to President Donald Trump’s construction projects after whistleblowers alleged that administration officials were destroying documents. The Interior Department called those allegations “100 percent false” and said it was complying with federal records-management requirements.

Reyes also temporarily halted major work at the Potomac East Golf Course and required advance notice before work proceeded. According to the report, more than 400 trees were cut down after officials notified the court through a filing submitted at 4:55 p.m. on the Friday before a federal holiday weekend.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Democratic lawmakers preparing to chair House committees planned preservation letters and possible subpoenas concerning the projects. Rep. Jared Huffman said the House Natural Resources Committee was prepared to litigate if the administration obstructed its oversight.

Power was already being exercised

The central fact is not that Democrats wrote stern letters. The administration controlled the agencies, the records and the work site. Officials could authorize construction, determine how notice was delivered and retain—or potentially lose—the material Congress and the courts might later seek.

That imbalance explains Reyes’s order. A preservation directive is not punishment and does not establish that records were destroyed. It is an attempt to prevent the government’s control over evidence from making judicial review and congressional oversight meaningless.

Notice without accountability

The golf-course episode shows how formal compliance can defeat substantive oversight. A late-Friday filing before a holiday weekend may technically provide notice, but it leaves little practical opportunity for a court or opposing parties to respond before irreversible work begins.

More than 400 felled trees cannot be restored by a later hearing. When government action creates permanent facts on the ground faster than institutions can examine it, procedure becomes camouflage for power. Reyes’s temporary ban addressed that asymmetry directly by stopping the work rather than trusting paperwork alone.

Congress has tools, not guarantees

Huffman’s promised preservation demands, subpoenas and litigation matter because committees possess institutional authority that individual whistleblowers do not. The relevant question is whether Congress will use that authority quickly enough to secure records before delay, resistance or administrative churn renders oversight academic.

The article’s “winter is coming” flourish is less important than the machinery behind it. Committee jurisdiction, compulsory process and standing to sue are the actual leverage. Oversight succeeds through enforceable deadlines and consequences, not ominous quotations.

The weaker actors are not the story

Whistleblowers triggered scrutiny, but they did not control federal records or construction decisions. Framing the dispute chiefly as a clash between anonymous accusers and an agency denial would misplace responsibility. The agencies holding the documents bear the legal obligation to preserve them, while administration officials exercising delegated power bear responsibility for how public projects proceed.

The Interior Department’s denial remains part of the factual record, and the reported allegations remain allegations. But that dispute does not erase the institutional problem: the executive branch cannot be the sole judge of whether evidence concerning its own conduct survives for review.

Oversight after the bulldozers

This story reveals a recurring weakness in American oversight. Executive action can move at operational speed; courts and Congress usually move through notices, hearings and litigation. An administration benefits from that gap whenever irreversible action is completed before review arrives.

The systemic issue is therefore larger than one golf course or one preservation order. Government accountability depends on institutions securing evidence and stopping consequential action while scrutiny is still possible. Once the records disappear or the landscape is altered, oversight may document the damage—but it no longer prevents it.

Source: AlterNet

item.title: Low attendance a problem for White House as GOP bails on sinking ship
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that House Republicans expected to lose Tuesday’s vote on Rep. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Twenty-two Republicans were reportedly absent from Washington after the November 3 election losses, and few were expected to return to Congress in 2027, leaving the party without the attendance needed to control the vote.
