item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Detroit pastor Lorenzo Sewell called for “another January 6” after Democratic candidates reportedly defeated Republicans in several major midterm races. Appearing on the “FlashPoint” podcast, Sewell alleged fraud, said he was preparing to go to the Capitol, and claimed he and unnamed friends were ready to present evidence.

His stated basis was that Republican candidates carried more counties in Michigan, Texas, and Ohio while Democrats won the statewide contests. That comparison ignores the number of voters in each county: counties do not cast ballots, people do. Sewell nevertheless described his suspicion as spiritually inspired and cast the reported Republican losses as theft by political and demonic enemies.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

AlterNet identifies Sewell as the leader of Detroit’s 180 Church, a 2024 Republican National Convention speaker, and a participant in Donald Trump’s 2025 inauguration. The article does not report that Sewell specified what form “another January 6” should take beyond traveling to the Capitol and presenting purported evidence.

The arithmetic is not the mistake

Sewell’s county-count argument is elementary nonsense, but treating it merely as confusion misses its political function. Sparse counties do not acquire extra votes because they occupy more acreage or appear more frequently on a map. A candidate can win many lightly populated counties and still lose statewide because the other candidate received more votes.

The argument replaces equal citizenship with territorial entitlement. It suggests that Republican geography should outweigh Democratic population—and that an election becomes suspect when cities and populous suburbs determine the result. The grievance is not really that votes were counted incorrectly. No such evidence appears in AlterNet’s account. The grievance is that the wrong voters were allowed to decide.

A pastor with political access

Sewell is not described as an isolated congregant muttering online. He has spoken at a Republican National Convention, delivered a benediction at a presidential inauguration, and reportedly considered seeking office as a Republican. Those connections do not make him a government decision-maker, but they do give him a platform inside a movement with institutional power.

The actual power remains with party officials, elected leaders, media operators, and political organizations that decide which voices receive access and legitimacy. Sewell supplied the rhetoric; the Republican political ecosystem helped build the audience. Elevating election conspiracists and then treating their escalation as an eccentric personal outburst obscures how that influence was accumulated.

Theology as political permission

Calling an unsupported suspicion a “Holy Ghost hunch” launders a partisan demand through religious authority. Sewell did not merely dispute reported outcomes. He framed Democratic victories as theft, declared Trump’s presidency effectively finished, and told Christians to “reclaim” what the devil had taken.

That formulation strips political opponents of ordinary legitimacy. Democrats become agents of evil; unfavorable results become proof of fraud; resistance becomes a sacred obligation. This is Christian nationalism performing one of its central political tasks: converting the loss of power into persecution and retaliation into faithfulness.

The January 6 reference is the point

“Another January 6” is not politically neutral shorthand for filing paperwork. Sewell paired the phrase with mobilization, the Capitol, alleged theft, and a claim that the president’s authority had been destroyed. AlterNet does not establish that he explicitly called for violence, and his stated action was to present supposed evidence. But the reference deliberately invokes an attempt to overturn an election through pressure at the seat of government.

The danger in the rhetoric lies in the sequence it normalizes: declare fraud without demonstrated proof, portray legal electoral defeat as national dispossession, and summon supporters to confront the institutions recognizing the result. Even when phrased ambiguously, that script teaches an audience that elections bind only the opposition.

Defeat becomes illegitimate by definition

The larger pattern is a movement training itself to recognize only victories as valid. When Republicans win, the system expresses the people’s will. When Democrats win populous jurisdictions and take statewide offices, colored county maps become an excuse to allege theft.

That is not election skepticism. It is minority-rule ideology with a religious gloss. Sewell’s remarks reveal the consequence of years spent rewarding conspiracy claims: ordinary vote counting becomes intolerable whenever it denies the movement power. The fraud allegation then ceases to be a claim requiring evidence. It becomes a standing permission slip to reject democratic loss.

item.title: Behind Vance’s new pivot —and the Paypal Mafia's plot to repackage Trumpism
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Vice President JD Vance responded to significant Republican midterm losses with an extended post on X arguing that disillusioned Trump voters wanted four things: an end to the war, relief from inflation and living costs, an “America First” agenda, and a changed relationship with Israel. Although some interpreted the statement as a rebuke of President Donald Trump, Vance did not renounce the administration or its governing project. Instead, Vance urged dissatis
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Vice President JD Vance responded to significant Republican midterm losses with an extended post on X arguing that disillusioned Trump voters wanted four things: an end to the war, relief from inflation and living costs, an “America First” agenda, and a changed relationship with Israel. Although some interpreted the statement as a rebuke of President Donald Trump, Vance did not renounce the administration or its governing project.

Instead, Vance urged dissatisfied voters to elect Republicans who shared their views. AlterNet presents that appeal as an early effort to rebuild the party’s coalition—and potentially prepare for Vance’s own 2028 ambitions—by adopting the language of anti-war and economic discontent without abandoning the interests and policies that produced it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The outlet ties this maneuver to Vance’s political relationship with billionaire Peter Thiel and a broader network of technology, surveillance, and military contractors. Its central claim is that Vance’s pivot represents a change in salesmanship, not a transfer of power or a demonstrated change in policy.

The diagnosis comes from inside the administration

Vance speaks as if he were an outside analyst studying a mysterious collapse. He is not. As vice president, he holds institutional power inside the administration whose war policy, economic record, and support for Israel he now identifies as electoral liabilities.

That distinction matters. Vance did not merely observe these outcomes; he helped defend the governing coalition responsible for them. His invitation to have an “honest conversation” converts accountability into consultation. Voters are asked to explain their suffering to officials who already recognize it well enough to incorporate it into campaign strategy.

The supposed candor is therefore limited. Naming an unpopular condition is not the same as accepting responsibility for creating or sustaining it. No policy reversal is established in the reporting. What Vance offers is recognition without remedy.

Populism as a retrieval operation

The post’s operative instruction is not “change the government’s conduct.” It is “elect Republicans who share your worldview.” That turns public anger into a voter-recovery program for the party currently exercising executive power.

Anti-war language is especially useful because it can be narrowed to opposition to one conflict while leaving the larger military and contracting apparatus intact. Economic populism can likewise be reduced to grocery and fuel prices while avoiding concentrated ownership, taxation, deregulation, and the transfer of public resources into private hands.

This is how political appropriation works: acknowledge the grievance, detach it from its institutional cause, and redirect the injured constituency toward the same power structure. The promise changes faster than the policy because rhetoric is cheap and governing commitments are not.

The patrons outlast the branding

AlterNet emphasizes Vance’s history with Thiel as employer, mentor, donor, and political patron. That relationship is politically relevant because it identifies a durable center of power beneath the candidate’s changing presentation: wealthy technology interests seeking government contracts, deregulation, privatization, and expanded markets for surveillance, artificial intelligence, and weapons systems.

The article makes a broader point that should not be obscured by speculation about a personal break with Trump. Trump is a vehicle for a coalition of billionaire networks, contractors, reactionary organizers, and political operators; he is not the coalition itself. Those interests can tolerate different personalities and contradictory slogans so long as access, accumulation, and coercive state capacity remain available.

Vance’s pivot is coherent within that structure. A politician can promise economic relief while serving concentrated wealth, or invoke peace while backed by industries that benefit from state violence. The contradiction belongs to the voter-facing message, not to the interests financing it.

Misdirection has willing accomplices

Reading Vance’s post as proof of moderation shifts attention from decisions to tone. It rewards an official for accurately describing damage that his own administration reportedly helped produce. That is not introspection; at most, it is competent threat assessment by a governing faction facing electoral losses.

AlterNet also contrasts this Republican recalibration with a Democratic establishment inclined to treat rejection of Trump as endorsement of its own leadership. The comparison is useful insofar as it identifies a shared evasion: party elites interpret elections as permission to preserve themselves, while voters’ material demands are reduced to branding data.

The weaker actors here are the voters being courted, not the officials studying how to recover them. Blaming public confusion or partisan volatility would invert the power relationship. Political organizations with money, institutional access, and control over policy are designing the choices; the electorate is being offered revised packaging.

The system learns faster than it changes

The larger pattern is not that Trumpism has discovered humility. It is that an elite coalition can shed a damaged persona, absorb the vocabulary of its critics, and continue pursuing the same distribution of power.

Electoral defeat may force tactical adaptation without producing structural concession. Vance’s statement shows a governing faction recognizing that war, economic insecurity, and unconditional alignment with Israel carry political costs. It does not show that the faction has accepted the policies required to reverse them.

That is the systemic error: treating responsive language as responsive government. Power has not moved merely because its custodians have updated the pitch.

item.title: Haberman spills new details about Trump's behind-the-scenes meltdown
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Maggie Haberman told CNN that President Donald Trump berated White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in the East Room on Election Night and blamed her for sweeping Republican midterm losses. Haberman said Trump had criticized Wiles privately, publicly within the administration, and to her face for at least six months before replacing her with Stephen Miller. According to Haberman, Miller was not among those pressing for Wiles’s removal and reportedly had been c
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Maggie Haberman told CNN that President Donald Trump berated White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in the East Room on Election Night and blamed her for sweeping Republican midterm losses. Haberman said Trump had criticized Wiles privately, publicly within the administration, and to her face for at least six months before replacing her with Stephen Miller.

According to Haberman, Miller was not among those pressing for Wiles’s removal and reportedly had been comfortable with her remaining. She also said Trump had attacked Wiles over her failure to identify who leaked information about his travel to Turkey during a NATO summit, when officials allegedly misrepresented his whereabouts.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The power was always Trump’s

Wiles managed the White House, but Trump held the presidency, set its policy, and resisted being constrained. Haberman’s account therefore describes more than an angry boss firing a disappointing subordinate. It describes the country’s most powerful official assigning responsibility downward for political consequences produced under his own authority.

A wave extending, in Haberman’s description, from Mississippi to Maine cannot plausibly be reduced to one aide’s tactical mistakes. Voters were responding to a governing party and a president. Trump had the power to shape both. Wiles became useful precisely because she did not.

A scapegoat, not an explanation

Blaming Wiles converts a broad electoral rejection into a personnel failure. That misdirection protects Trump from the central implication of the results: Republican losses across disparate states may reflect opposition to the administration’s leadership and policies, not merely defective political management.

The distinction matters. Staff can influence scheduling, communications, and campaign execution. They cannot erase presidential responsibility for an administration whose policy, Haberman emphasized, was largely set by the president. Treating Wiles as the cause confuses proximity to power with possession of it.

Humiliation as management

Trump reportedly did not merely dismiss Wiles. He berated her before others and had spent months criticizing her while people inside the administration undermined her. That is a governing structure built around personal favor, internal rivalry, and the leader’s anger—not clear lines of accountability.

The fixation on finding the Turkey-travel leak sharpens the point. In Haberman’s account, Trump was furious that Wiles had not identified whoever exposed an alleged official deception about his whereabouts. The institutional priority was apparently not examining why officials misled people, but locating the person who revealed it. That is how secrecy becomes loyalty and truth-telling becomes betrayal.

Miller changes the personnel, not the structure

Stephen Miller’s elevation may alter who executes Trump’s agenda, but it does not relocate presidential agency. Haberman specifically said Miller was not driving Wiles’s ouster. The decisive actor was Trump, who had soured on his chief of staff and ultimately replaced her.

The danger in focusing chiefly on Miller’s reputation is that it can again shift attention away from the officeholder making the choice. Miller may wield substantial delegated influence, but Trump selected him, narrowed the decision-making circle, and rejected restraint. The structure is personal rule exercised through chosen loyalists.

Failure flows downward

This episode reveals a recurring pattern of personalized power: authority concentrates at the top while blame is distributed beneath it. Success validates the leader; failure incriminates advisers, disloyal officials, leakers, or insufficiently obedient managers.

That arrangement does more than produce a toxic workplace. It prevents electoral defeat from functioning as political feedback. When the person setting policy treats rejection as evidence that subordinates failed him, accountability becomes impossible by design—and the next response is likely to be greater loyalty, tighter secrecy, and fewer people empowered to say no.

item.title: Report exposes Trump’s surreal behavior behind closed doors after shellacking
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump responded to Republicans’ landslide defeat in the 2026 midterms with denial rather than public acknowledgment. Citing New York Times reporter Peter Baker, it describes Trump as “flat,” possibly dazed, and largely unwilling to recognize the electorate’s rejection while his party assessed its losses. Trump signed a beam for a new White House ballroom, traveled to Florida for a space-program speech, and offered no concession comparable to G
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump responded to Republicans’ landslide defeat in the 2026 midterms with denial rather than public acknowledgment. Citing New York Times reporter Peter Baker, it describes Trump as “flat,” possibly dazed, and largely unwilling to recognize the electorate’s rejection while his party assessed its losses.

Trump signed a beam for a new White House ballroom, traveled to Florida for a space-program speech, and offered no concession comparable to George W. Bush’s “thumping” or Barack Obama’s “shellacking.” Meanwhile, the White House posted, “TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT,” as Trump faced the erosion of influence that commonly follows a president’s loss of congressional power.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Political analyst Allan Lichtman told AlterNet that the scale of the result invited comparisons with the congressional upheavals of 1994 and 1894. He attributed the 2026 rout partly to a sour economy and partly to an unpopular war, which he treated as a separate political liability.

The headline overpromises

The reporting does not expose much “behind closed doors.” Its evidence is chiefly Trump’s public schedule, his failure to acknowledge the defeat, a White House message, and Baker’s interpretation of his demeanor. No private remark or concealed episode establishes the headline’s promised surreal behavior.

That distinction matters. Trump’s internal emotional state is less politically important than his official response. Calling him dazed risks converting an exercise of presidential agency into a psychological spectacle. Whatever Trump privately feels, he chose not to acknowledge public discontent, and his White House chose to answer repudiation with an assertion of continuing status.

Power did not disappear

Republicans lost congressional power, but Trump remained president. The White House still controlled the executive branch, the machinery of administration, and the immense public authority attached to the office. “TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT” was therefore literally true, but politically revealing: it answered an electoral rebuke by emphasizing the power voters had not yet removed.

Institutional power does not vanish because its holder looks diminished. The election constrained Trump and weakened his leverage; it did not make him a bystander. Coverage centered on whether he seemed sad, stunned, or detached can obscure the more consequential question: how a repudiated president uses the authority he retains.

Denial is a governing choice

Bush and Obama publicly admitted major midterm losses. Trump reportedly did not. That contrast is not merely about humility or temperament. A president’s acknowledgment of defeat tells the governing party that voters imposed a constraint. Refusing that acknowledgment gives allies permission to treat the result as an inconvenience rather than an instruction.

The article notes that conservative groups were already arguing Republicans would have prevailed had Trump followed their advice. That is the familiar machinery of factional evasion: accept the vote count while rewriting its meaning so no one with power must accept responsibility. The president avoids the verdict; aligned organizations convert defeat into a tactical disagreement.

The electorate supplied the consequence

The decisive actors were voters, who stripped Trump’s party of congressional control amid economic dissatisfaction and opposition to war, according to Lichtman’s analysis. Trump dominated the political system for years, but dominance is not permanence. Once congressional majorities change hands, agenda control, oversight authority, and bargaining power change with them.

Historical analogies cannot establish what follows. The 1894 rout preceded a long Republican era, but Lichtman also identified important differences in economic conditions. The sound conclusion is narrower: this was a large transfer of institutional power, not proof of a settled political realignment.

The system rewards spectacle over accountability

The larger pattern is political journalism’s attraction to the ruler’s mood after the public has acted. A devastated party, a lost Congress, an unpopular war, and economic discontent become scenery for a personality study: Was Trump dazed? Could he admit his era was ending?

That frame shrinks democratic power into presidential psychology. The consequential story is not that Trump may have struggled emotionally with defeat. It is that voters imposed a material limit, the White House answered with defiance, and Republican interests began repositioning themselves without squarely accepting responsibility. The spectacle is his demeanor. The politics is the fight over whether an electoral judgment will constrain those who still hold power.

item.title: The College Admissions Circus: What America Could Learn From Brazil
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: American universities are panicking because students who promised to attend are disappearing. Meanwhile, Brazilian colleges have a rather revolutionary approach: enroll the student and start teaching. The Great American Disappearing Student American universities have discovered a terrifying new phenomenon: students who say they'll attend college sometimes change their minds. Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself: ☕ Buy us a coffee Apparently, this requires a name, a strate
item.content:encoded:
American universities are panicking because students who promised to attend are disappearing. Meanwhile, Brazilian colleges have a rather revolutionary approach: enroll the student and start teaching.

The Great American Disappearing Student

American universities have discovered a terrifying new phenomenon: students who say they'll attend college sometimes change their minds.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Apparently, this requires a name, a strategy, and possibly an entire administrative department.

In a November 2026 Wall Street Journal article, “Colleges Struggle to Stop ‘Melt’: Students Who Commit, Then Don't Show Up”, reporter Roshan Fernandez describes a growing headache for American institutions.

Students accept admission offers, pay deposits, and then fail to appear when classes begin.

The colleges call this summer melt.

At Whittier College in California, 17% of students who had committed failed to show up. Some institutions are experiencing rates approaching 20%.

Meanwhile, students entering college in 2025 placed an average of 1.4 enrollment deposits, compared with approximately one in 2019.

Universities are responding with what they call freeze strategies: increasingly elaborate efforts to keep students engaged, committed, and emotionally attached to their chosen institution throughout the summer.

Faculty outreach. Personalized messages. Financial-aid counseling. Parent engagement. Orientation programs. Registration assistance.

All designed to prevent a student from committing the apparently unforgivable offense of taking their business elsewhere.

And somewhere in Brazil, a college administrator is probably wondering what all the fuss is about.

Meanwhile, in Brazil…

Imagine the following conversation at a typical, less-selective Brazilian private college.

Student: “I'd like to enroll.”

Administrator: “Certainly. Which degree program?”

Student: “Computer Science.”

Administrator: “Excellent. Here's the required documentation, the enrollment procedure, and your tuition. Classes begin next month.”

Student: “Here's my payment.”

Administrator: “Welcome to the college.”

End of story.

Naturally, there are formal admission requirements. Brazilian institutions cannot simply enroll anyone who walks through the door without satisfying educational and regulatory prerequisites.

But for many private colleges, those requirements are straightforward, and the admission process is designed to facilitate enrollment rather than transform it into an elaborate ceremony of institutional approval.

This is not a fringe characteristic of Brazilian higher education.

According to the 2026 Mapa do Ensino Superior, based on government education data, approximately 79.8% of Brazilian higher-education enrollment is in private institutions.

And those institutions have a very practical understanding of their relationship with prospective students.

They provide education. Students pay tuition.

The institution's responsibility is to establish whether applicants qualify, admit them when places are available, and deliver the education they purchased.

A remarkably uncomplicated arrangement.

Brazil Has Competitive Admissions. It Just Doesn't Confuse Them With a Personality Contest.

None of this means Brazilian universities have abandoned competitive admissions.

Far from it.

For decades, Brazilian students aspiring to prestigious institutions have faced the vestibular, an entrance examination that can be exceptionally demanding.

The University of São Paulo (USP) uses FUVEST. The University of Campinas (Unicamp) maintains its own examination. Other institutions have adopted national examination results or hybrid admission systems.

The national examination, ENEM (Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio), has increasingly become a gateway to higher education.

Through SISU (Sistema de Seleção Unificada), students compete for places at participating public institutions using their examination results.

Other programs use ENEM scores to determine scholarship or financing eligibility.

Even prestigious private universities can offer relatively straightforward admission routes. PUC-SP, for example, offered a 2026 supplemental admissions process based exclusively on ENEM scores.

Here's the crucial distinction.

Brazilian universities generally ask students to demonstrate academic eligibility and compete for available places. Many American universities additionally ask students to demonstrate why their personal histories make them worthy of admission.

In the American system, depending on the institution, applicants may need standardized test results, recommendation letters, extracurricular records, personal essays, supplementary essays, interviews, and financial-aid documentation.

The Common Application makes much of this easier to coordinate, but individual institutions can still impose their own combinations of requirements.

The applicant isn't merely demonstrating academic preparation.

They're selling a biography.

Somehow, American higher education decided that becoming a college student should sometimes resemble applying for a senior executive position at a Fortune 500 company.

And this raises an uncomfortable question:

How much of that complexity actually measures educational potential, and how much exists to reinforce the institution's perception of its own importance?

When Difficulty Becomes Prestige

There is a psychological trick at work in American higher education.

When something is difficult to obtain, people tend to assume it must be valuable.

Universities have spent generations cultivating this association.

Acceptance rates become bragging rights. Rejection becomes evidence of exclusivity. Admissions offices proudly announce record application numbers, even when the number of available places has barely changed.

An institution rejecting 95% of applicants sounds impressive.

But rejection itself doesn't educate anyone.

A university's acceptance rate tells us how many applicants it rejected relative to its applicant pool. It doesn't directly tell us how well its professors teach, how rigorous its examinations are, or how competent its graduates become.

An institution can reject thousands of qualified applicants and still deliver mediocre instruction.

Another can admit most qualified applicants and demand substantial academic achievement before awarding a diploma.

These are not contradictory possibilities.

They're different measurements.

Selectivity measures access. Academic rigor measures expectations. Educational quality measures something more complicated: what students actually learn.

Yet the American prestige economy frequently encourages people to treat these concepts as interchangeable.

And once complexity becomes associated with prestige, institutions have an incentive to preserve it, whether or not it serves students.

I suspect that some less-prestigious universities imitate elite admissions practices partly because those practices make an institution appear more selective.

That is an interpretation, not a universal diagnosis of administrators' intentions. But the prestige incentive is hardly imaginary.

For years, acceptance rates were included in the U.S. News college ranking methodology before being removed in 2018.

When rejection itself becomes a metric of success, the incentives are already upside down.

Brazilʼs Other Extreme: “Pagou, Passou”

Before anybody mistakes this for an advertisement for Brazilian higher education, we should acknowledge the country's own longstanding educational dysfunction.

Brazil has an expression for certain private colleges:

“Pagou, passou.”

Roughly translated: “You pay, you pass.”

It's the Brazilian version of a diploma mill.

For decades, some institutions have faced reputational criticism for prioritizing tuition revenue over educational standards.

The economic temptation is obvious.

If students are paying customers, failing them can be bad for business. A student who fails repeatedly may leave, transferring their tuition payments elsewhere.

The result can be pressure to keep paying students progressing regardless of whether they've adequately mastered the material.

But notice something important.

That failure has almost nothing to do with how difficult admission was.

It concerns what happens after enrollment.

Brazil also has respected private universities, including the Pontifical Catholic Universities, whose academic reputations demonstrate that accessible admission pathways and serious educational standards can coexist.

And even within those institutions, admission competitiveness varies substantially by program.

A university need not reject nearly every applicant to take education seriously.

Conversely, an extraordinarily selective institution is not automatically immune to grade inflation, lenient grading, or inadequate teaching.

The relevant question isn't how difficult it was to enter.

It's whether the institution is prepared to withhold a diploma from someone who hasn't earned it.

The proper measure of academic seriousness is not how many students you reject before classes begin, but what you require students to accomplish before graduation.

The Financial Reality Behind America's “Melt”

Returning to the original Wall Street Journal story, there's an even more revealing problem with the term summer melt.

It combines fundamentally different circumstances into one convenient administrative category.

A student who accepts an offer from University A and subsequently receives a better financial-aid package from University B isn't experiencing an educational crisis.

They're making an economic decision.

A student who intends to enroll but discovers that tuition, accommodation, or family circumstances make attendance impossible is facing a genuine financial barrier.

And a student who gets lost in a labyrinth of financial-aid forms, registration procedures, documentation requirements, and institutional deadlines is encountering an administrative failure.

These problems require entirely different responses.

Yet calling all three “melt” allows universities to describe them collectively as students disappearing.

Consider the competitive version.

American colleges routinely admit more students than they expect to attend. They calculate enrollment yields, maintain waiting lists, and compete for prospective applicants.

This is considered sophisticated enrollment management.

But when students place deposits at multiple institutions to preserve their options, administrators suddenly face an enrollment emergency.

Apparently, the university is permitted to hedge its bets.

The student, however, is expected to behave as though an acceptance letter were a marriage proposal.

There's a certain hypocrisy in that expectation.

American higher education has embraced market competition, elaborate tuition pricing, selective financial aid, and institutional branding.

Students have simply learned to behave like market participants.

If University B offers a better deal than University A, why shouldn't a student take it?

A diploma is an investment. For many American families, an extremely expensive one.

Prestige doesn't pay the bills.

When Bureaucracy Becomes the Obstacle

One of the most revealing examples in the original article involves Georgia State University.

The institution reportedly reduced its melt rate from 22% in 2024 to approximately 7% by simplifying registration and improving communication and support.

That's a remarkable improvement.

And it suggests that at least some students weren't abandoning higher education because they suddenly became irresponsible or unreliable.

They were failing to complete a complicated transition.

When institutions help students navigate that transition, more students show up.

Imagine that.

A university discovers that making enrollment easier increases enrollment.

Revolutionary.

Brazilian universities certainly have their own bureaucratic nightmares. Anyone who has dealt with Brazilian institutional paperwork knows that administrative absurdity is hardly an American monopoly.

But the widespread availability of relatively direct admission and enrollment pathways in Brazilian private higher education demonstrates that much of the elaborate American admissions experience isn't an unavoidable feature of university education.

It is a choice, shaped by institutional priorities, competition, financial structures, and tradition.

And choices can be changed.

A Personal Example: Back to College After Three Decades

I can offer a firsthand example of just how straightforward this process can be.

I'm currently pursuing my second bachelor's degree in Brazil, at the very same institution where I earned my first one more than thirty years ago.

Despite already holding a degree and having decades of professional experience, I enrolled as an ordinary incoming freshman, exactly as though I had just graduated from high school.

I went to the admissions office during the winter break, in the middle of the academic year, and asked about tuition and entrance examinations. After all, it had been more than three decades since I'd last gone through the process.

They directed me to the college's website, where I completed the application and paid the enrollment fee electronically. I was then scheduled for an entrance examination.

On examination day, I was handed a sheet of paper and asked to write an essay on a particular subject.

I couldn't tell you what that subject was today. I've completely forgotten it.

I wrote the required number of words, handed in the essay, and went home.

The following day, I received a notification informing me that I'd been accepted and inviting me to finalize my enrollment.

I returned to the admissions office, paid my tuition, and was told when classes would begin.

That was it.

No recommendation letters. No autobiographical essays about the adversity I'd overcome. No interviews about my ambitions, my character, or what unique perspective I might contribute to the student body.

And certainly no months-long campaign by the university to keep me from mysteriously “melting” before the semester began.

To be clear, this wasn't some obscure diploma mill desperate to collect tuition payments. It was Centro Universitário Fundação Santo André, a well-established, nonprofit institution with roots dating to 1953, created through municipal initiative and operating under the unusual legal structure of a public foundation governed by private law. It has a long academic tradition in São Paulo's industrial ABC region and has earned the highest institutional evaluation score awarded by Brazil's Ministry of Education.

And yet, despite its history, institutional credentials, and academic reputation, enrolling was remarkably straightforward.

The institution apparently understood something that many American universities struggle with: making admission unnecessarily complicated doesn't make an education more valuable.

But that's precisely the point.

The institution established that I satisfied its admission requirements, offered me a place, and enrolled me.

The entire process, from entrance examination to acceptance, took approximately twenty-four hours.

My previous degree didn't exempt me from the process. My professional experience didn't earn me preferential treatment.

And neither needed to.

I wanted to study. The college had a place available. I met its requirements.

Everything else could happen in the classroom, where education is supposed to take place.

The Comparison America Doesn't Want to Make

There are important differences between the two countries.

Brazilian public universities are generally tuition-free and frequently highly competitive. The United States has community colleges and less-selective institutions that also provide relatively straightforward admission.

Brazilian private institutions have their own financial pressures, and dropping out because of tuition or personal circumstances is hardly unusual.

Neither country has solved equitable access to higher education.

But comparing the systems reveals something worth examining.

In Brazil, the prestige of an institution can derive from academic tradition, examination performance, research, professional reputation, and the achievements of its graduates.

In the United States, those factors also matter, but the selectivity of the admissions process has become a particularly visible part of the prestige narrative.

The institution's ability to say “No” is treated as evidence of its value.

And that creates a peculiar relationship with students.

First, the university constructs an elaborate process requiring applicants to demonstrate why they deserve admission.

Then it congratulates those who survive the process.

Then it asks for a deposit.

And finally, when the student finds a better opportunity or encounters an insurmountable obstacle, it expresses astonishment that the commitment wasn't permanent.

The institution has spent months acting as though the applicant should feel privileged to be admitted.

Now it must spend the summer convincing that same applicant that attendance is worthwhile.

There's something almost poetic about the reversal.

Education Is Not an Exclusive Club

The purpose of a university should be to educate.

That sounds obvious, but higher education has developed an extraordinary capacity to complicate the obvious.

Admissions selectivity can serve legitimate purposes. Universities with limited places need mechanisms for choosing among qualified candidates. Competitive examinations, academic records, and other indicators can help make those decisions.

But complexity should have to justify itself.

If an additional essay, interview, recommendation, or administrative requirement doesn't meaningfully improve student selection, access, or educational outcomes, why impose it?

If a student meets the academic requirements, can secure a place, and is prepared to attend, why construct unnecessary obstacles?

And if institutions are struggling to retain students who have already accepted offers, perhaps they should begin by asking whether their own procedures, prices, and expectations are driving those students away.

The lesson from Brazil isn't that universities should admit everybody or hand out diplomas in exchange for tuition.

The lesson is considerably simpler.

Make it straightforward for qualified students to enter. Make the education worth attending. And make the diploma mean something when they leave.

American universities have become extraordinarily accomplished at measuring how difficult they are to enter.

Perhaps it's time they devoted comparable attention to demonstrating why students should want to stay.

After all, a university's purpose isn't to collect applications, celebrate rejection rates, or manufacture institutional mystique.

It's to teach.

And if a student finds a better educational opportunity somewhere else, that isn't necessarily a crisis.

Sometimes that's just competition.

Welcome to the market you've spent decades building.

item.title: Right-wing Newsmax gets 'blunt' lesson on Trump’s role in GOP's implosion
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Newsmax guests John Zogby and Patrick Allocco attributed a sweeping Republican election defeat—including losses of House and Senate majorities and a reported Democratic flip of Texas—to voter anxiety about affordability and Donald Trump’s political liability. Zogby called the result “an undeniable referendum” on the president, arguing that Trump emphasized projects such as arches, ballrooms, and reflecting pools while voters feared losing their middle-class st
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Newsmax guests John Zogby and Patrick Allocco attributed a sweeping Republican election defeat—including losses of House and Senate majorities and a reported Democratic flip of Texas—to voter anxiety about affordability and Donald Trump’s political liability. Zogby called the result “an undeniable referendum” on the president, arguing that Trump emphasized projects such as arches, ballrooms, and reflecting pools while voters feared losing their middle-class status.

Allocco said Democratic margins appeared unexpectedly strong even in House districts Trump had carried comfortably. Newsmax host Kyle Lowder, speaking after Republican Senator Susan Collins reportedly lost in Maine, conceded that Trump’s claims about a historically strong economy sounded patronizing beside voters’ material concerns. The article does not provide official results, vote totals, election dates, or independent evidence establishing how much Trump caused the losses.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Power wrote the message

Trump held the presidency, commanded the Republican Party’s national platform, and possessed the largest megaphone in its coalition. He was not a spectator whose messaging happened to collide with an unfavorable economy. According to Zogby’s account, he promised improvement in 2024 and later answered dissatisfaction with excuses and blame directed at Joe Biden.

That distinction matters. Presidents cannot control every price or household balance sheet, but they do choose what to prioritize and what reality to describe. Trump chose triumphal economic claims and ceremonial projects while voters were reportedly preoccupied with declining security. The institutional power belonged to him and the governing party. So did the political exposure.

Newsmax discovers accountability

The remarkable feature is not that analysts connected a governing president to his party’s losses. That is elementary political analysis. The remarkable feature is that Newsmax’s usual treatment of Trump made such an acknowledgment appear exceptional.

A media operation that habitually protects a leader eventually loses the ability to describe ordinary cause and effect without staging it as a startling revelation. Lowder’s concession arrived only after voters had allegedly imposed consequences too large to explain away. This was not fearless scrutiny. It was delayed recognition under electoral pressure.

Demography is context, not absolution

Zogby pointed to Texas’s growth, an influx of younger residents and knowledge-sector suburbanites, and the emergence of what he called a “new Texas.” Those shifts may help explain why the state became more competitive. They do not erase the reported national movement across places including Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, and Maine.

Demographic explanation can become a convenient escape hatch: the electorate changed, the map changed, history arrived. But voters still respond to governing records, economic claims, candidates, and party brands. Structural change created vulnerability; political choices reportedly converted it into defeat.

The weaker actors did not govern

The framing risks turning the result into a mysterious “blue wave,” as though electoral weather swept through without authors. Waves are metaphors. Officeholders set priorities, parties defend them, and aligned media outlets tell voters which facts should count.

The people fearing the loss of middle-class status did not create the contradiction between official celebration and lived insecurity. Nor did new Texas residents single-handedly damage the Republican brand nationwide. The account points upward: to a president selling prosperity, a party organized around him, and a friendly network that resisted naming the liability until the losses became unavoidable.

Propaganda fails at the checkout line

The larger pattern is the decay of a political information system built to flatter power. It can repeat that the economy is magnificent, redirect blame to a predecessor, and treat presidential vanity projects as governing substance. What it cannot do is make household insecurity disappear.

When material experience defeats the approved story, loyal media often presents the rupture as sudden public confusion or an unforeseeable wave. AlterNet’s account suggests something more concrete: voters recognized a gap between presidential claims and their own circumstances, then punished the party holding power. Newsmax’s “blunt” lesson was merely the bill for refusing to say so earlier.

item.title: Multibillion-dollar battle brewing behind closed doors will affect every American
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, republishing KFF Health News, reports that the 2026 midterms strengthened Democrats who support some form of Medicare for All, but did not produce a congressional majority clearly committed to replacing private insurance. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed campaigned on a plan that would guarantee baseline government coverage while allowing employer and union plans to remain. The immediate fight is over how Democrats respond to rising costs. The article says enhanced Affordable
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, republishing KFF Health News, reports that the 2026 midterms strengthened Democrats who support some form of Medicare for All, but did not produce a congressional majority clearly committed to replacing private insurance. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed campaigned on a plan that would guarantee baseline government coverage while allowing employer and union plans to remain.

The immediate fight is over how Democrats respond to rising costs. The article says enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired at the end of 2025, premiums are expected to rise by double digits in 2027, and looming Medicaid cuts are projected to leave 7.5 million more people uninsured by 2034. Options range from restoring subsidies and restricting prior authorization to creating a public option or broader universal coverage.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Patients already face the consequences. Former nurse Jaime Bardenhagen said her family’s monthly premium rose from $700 to $1,300, alongside a $7,500 deductible, leading them to postpone medical tests. Emergency nurse Kim Bogan described patients arriving sicker, unable to afford prescriptions, while understaffing forces her to care for five or six people at once.

Who holds the power

Patients possess urgency, not institutional power. Nurses can describe preventable suffering. Voters can punish incumbents. Neither group writes federal legislation, sets reimbursement rates, approves insurance claims, or decides whether millions retain Medicaid coverage.

Congress and the federal government hold the formal authority. Insurers, drug companies, hospitals, and other healthcare businesses hold the concentrated money and organizational capacity to shape what Congress considers politically possible. Even Michael Cannon, a Medicare for All opponent at the Cato Institute, predicts that industry would dominate the system. His warning inadvertently identifies the central problem: corporate influence is already treated as a governing fact.

The decision is political

The affordability crisis did not arrive like bad weather. Public officials allowed enhanced ACA subsidies to expire. Insurers impose prior-authorization barriers. Employers shift growing premium costs onto workers. Federal policy determines whether Medicaid is expanded or cut.

Moderate Democrats described in the reporting may resist Medicare for All because they fear losing recently won seats in Republican-leaning states. That is a strategic choice: protect an electoral coalition by limiting reform, even as patients absorb higher premiums, delayed tests, and lost coverage. Political caution has beneficiaries, and they are rarely the people rationing care.

The framing protects the obstruction

The article repeatedly presents universal coverage as a risky “government takeover” that would require people to surrender existing insurance. But the status quo already subjects patients to remote authorities making binding decisions. Bardenhagen said insurers, rather than doctors, determined which prescriptions and procedures patients could receive.

Polling showing that support weakens when respondents hear warnings about taxes or treatment delays measures the effectiveness of those warnings; it does not establish that Medicare for All would produce either result. Nor do narrower victories by outspoken supporters prove that voters rejected universal coverage. As the article itself notes, inflation, corruption, and the Iran war also shaped the election.

The framing therefore risks relocating responsibility from institutions capable of blocking reform to voters portrayed as hesitant or ideologically conflicted. The multibillion-dollar battle is not merely a national debate over policy design. It is a struggle between diffuse public need and industries with direct financial stakes in preserving their authority.

Managed relief, preserved power

Restoring subsidies or limiting prior authorization could materially help patients. Those measures should not be dismissed simply because they fall short of structural reform. But subsidies can also route more public money through private insurers without dislodging them, while procedural restrictions leave the basic architecture of corporate control intact.

That is why “lowest-hanging fruit” is an revealing description. Congress gravitates toward reforms that reduce visible pain without confronting the institutions producing it. Patients receive temporary relief; incumbents claim action; dominant firms retain their position.

The system makes suffering negotiable

The larger pattern is a familiar one: severe public harm becomes evidence for reform, then concentrated power converts reform into a negotiation over how little must change. Nurses report dangerous workloads. Sick people delay tests. Millions face the prospect of losing coverage. Yet the political system treats the industry’s expected resistance as more decisive than those consequences.

The decisive question is not whether Americans are sufficiently patient, persuaded, or ideologically comfortable with government. It is whether elected officials will use their authority against organizations capable of financing opposition. Until they do, healthcare policy will continue to describe avoidable suffering as an affordability “crisis” while preserving the decisions and power structures that make care unaffordable.

item.title: The Reckoning: How Lindsey Graham’s ominous warning about Trump finally came true
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Lindsey Graham’s 2016 warning—that Republicans would be “destroyed” if they nominated Donald Trump—finally materialized in the 2026 midterms. Democrats won the national congressional popular vote by 13 percentage points, flipped more than 40 House seats, gained at least seven Senate seats, captured five governorships and took as many as 12 state legislative chambers. Republicans also lost Graham’s former South Carolina seat after his reported death in July. Th
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Lindsey Graham’s 2016 warning—that Republicans would be “destroyed” if they nominated Donald Trump—finally materialized in the 2026 midterms. Democrats won the national congressional popular vote by 13 percentage points, flipped more than 40 House seats, gained at least seven Senate seats, captured five governorships and took as many as 12 state legislative chambers. Republicans also lost Graham’s former South Carolina seat after his reported death in July.

The losses reached deep into Trump territory. Democrats won Ohio’s races for governor and Senate, captured four Republican-held House districts in Pennsylvania and prevailed in states where they had not won Senate contests for decades. AlterNet portrays the result as a delayed reckoning with Trump’s second-term record, including high prices, social-welfare cuts, aggressive immigration enforcement, alleged self-dealing and a war with Iran that the outlet says had already cost taxpayers more than $47 billion.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

At campaign stops in Ohio and Pennsylvania, the reporter found former Trump supporters turning against Republican candidates while some loyalists redirected responsibility toward Congress, markets or conspiracy theories. Trump, meanwhile, offered digressions, insults and self-praise at a diminished Ohio rally as voters described material pressures his administration and Republican allies had the power to address.

Power had nowhere left to hide

The governing hierarchy is not ambiguous. Trump held the presidency. Republicans controlled both houses of Congress. Republicans had governed Ohio since 2010. Their candidates could not credibly present themselves as outsiders confronting somebody else’s system.

Yet that is precisely the political habit Trumpism had cultivated: exercise state power while speaking as though an unnamed establishment remains in charge. Jacob Hawk blamed Congress for supposedly preventing domestic drilling, overlooking that Trump’s party controlled Congress. Debbie Shock blamed “the markets.” The confusion protected the officials making policy from the consequences voters were experiencing.

The central decision identified by AlterNet is Trump’s choice to enter the war with Iran. The article connects that decision to higher fuel prices and reports that Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth encouraged Trump’s swagger. But influence is not authority. Trump made the decision; Republican legislators enabled his administration; Republican candidates inherited the consequences.

The scapegoats were weaker than the rulers

Trump’s rally rhetoric pushed attention downward and outward: Haitians in Springfield, Somali people, transgender people, protesters, Democrats and Barack Obama’s supposed failure to understand “cleanliness.” None of those targets controlled the presidency, Congress or the war policy burdening the voters gathered before him.

That is not an accidental mismatch. The speech’s political function was displacement, whatever Trump’s personal intent: turn economic pain into resentment against immigrants, minorities and cultural enemies while the officials holding institutional power escape scrutiny. Even Jeffrey Epstein became material for partisan inversion, with Trump declaring himself exonerated and blaming Democrats rather than addressing the documented questions that had made the subject politically dangerous.

The result outside the arena showed the foreseeable consequence of such politics. Accusations of “pedophiles” flew between opposing groups, and a Trump supporter knocked a protester to the pavement. The article does not establish that Trump ordered or intended the assault. It does show a rally organized around humiliation and accusation producing a space where political hostility became physical violence.

Material failure broke the spell

The decisive opposition described in Pennsylvania was not a single ideological conversion. Voters named lost SNAP benefits, threatened Medicaid coverage, inflation, diesel prices, harsh ICE arrests, the Iran war and alleged self-dealing by Trump’s family and associates. One three-time Trump voter, identified only as Bill, voted Democratic to impose “gridlock” after concluding that Trump’s promises to drain corruption and avoid wars had been false.

This matters because personality politics endured until policy consequences became difficult to rationalize away. Loyalty survived rambling speeches, conspiracy theories and cruelty toward designated enemies. It weakened when voters could connect government decisions to grocery assistance, health coverage, fuel bills, foreign war and abuses of public office.

AlterNet’s strongest evidence is not that every voter reached the same moral judgment. It is that Republican power produced many distinct injuries, which converged electorally. The rout was cumulative accountability.

Graham warned, then enabled

Graham correctly predicted political destruction in 2016, according to the tweet quoted by AlterNet. He then joined much of his party in accommodating Trump. That history makes the warning less an act of courage than an abandoned diagnosis.

Republican officials understood the danger and chose proximity to power anyway. The party survived earlier opportunities for accountability: Trump’s narrow 2016 victory, the January 6 assault on the Capitol and Joe Biden’s decision to seek reelection in 2024. Each reprieve taught Republican officeholders that submission carried fewer immediate costs than resistance.

The 2026 defeat did not vindicate Graham as a dissident. It exposed him as part of the enabling structure he had once described. Foreseeing a wreck does not absolve someone who later helps keep the vehicle moving.

The reckoning was institutional

The temptation is to frame this as voters finally discovering Trump’s true character. That is too comforting and too narrow. The larger failure belonged to a party that possessed governing power, refused responsibility for its decisions and relied on scapegoats to absorb public anger.

The same system that elevated Trump also furnished compliant legislators, candidates willing to defend cruelty, officials prepared to redirect blame and voters trained to see every failure as sabotage by somebody weaker. The midterm results disrupted that arrangement, but an electoral rout is not self-correction. It is a penalty imposed after years of institutional consent.

Graham’s warning came true only after his party spent a decade ensuring that the eventual bill would be larger. The destruction was not fate, and Trump did not accomplish it alone. Republican leaders repeatedly chose access over restraint, obedience over accountability and propaganda over governing. The voters merely ended the grace period.

item.title: History warns a catastrophic economic crash could be next
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet does not establish that a catastrophic economic crash is next. It argues that such a rupture is possible, using Peter Turchin’s theory of political disintegration and Neil Howe’s generational-cycle framework to interpret an election the article describes as occurring “this week.” Its central claim is that extreme wealth concentration, declining state capacity, and working-class economic insecurity resemble conditions that preceded earlier crises. The article says Elon Musk
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet does not establish that a catastrophic economic crash is next. It argues that such a rupture is possible, using Peter Turchin’s theory of political disintegration and Neil Howe’s generational-cycle framework to interpret an election the article describes as occurring “this week.” Its central claim is that extreme wealth concentration, declining state capacity, and working-class economic insecurity resemble conditions that preceded earlier crises.

The article says Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion traceable dollars supporting right-wing candidates, while billionaire-funded groups and AIPAC poured money into other races. It maintains that this spending failed to overcome voter anger in some contests, then urges Democrats to reject the party’s neoliberal faction, embrace progressive economic policies, and confront Donald Trump rather than cooperate with him. The piece supplies no economic forecast, crash date, or evidence that collapse is imminent.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The power is concentrated

The institutional power described here belongs primarily to wealthy donors, corporate owners, elected officials, judges, and party leaders. Billionaires can finance campaigns and control major communications platforms. Congress writes tax and spending law. Presidents direct the executive branch. Courts determine which campaign-finance and labor restrictions survive. Democratic leaders decide whether their party will challenge that structure or accommodate it.

Ordinary voters possess electoral agency, but they do not enter politics with equivalent leverage. Treating a ballot cast amid concentrated media ownership, enormous campaign spending, weakened unions, and economic precarity as an isolated consumer preference hides the machinery shaping the available choices.

The article is strongest when it names that imbalance. It is weaker when it compresses decades of institutional change into a single story of “the morbidly rich.” Wealth is not self-executing. Tax reductions, benefit cuts, anti-union laws, deregulation, and campaign-finance rules require officials to enact them and judges to sustain them. Oligarchic influence works through public institutions whose occupants retain responsibility for their decisions.

Democrats still have agency

The piece correctly refuses to portray Democratic leaders as helpless spectators. According to AlterNet, figures such as Chuck Schumer and Claire McCaskill represent a choice to seek cooperation or ideological moderation, while politicians including Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ro Khanna, Mark Pocan, and Abdul El-Sayed represent a more confrontational economic program.

That dispute is not merely about messaging. Party leaders control committee assignments, legislative priorities, campaign resources, endorsements, and the boundaries of acceptable policy. When they favor affluent donors or dilute broadly popular economic proposals, they are exercising power—not bowing to an unexplained political weather system.

But the article overstates what polling alone can prove. Support for Medicare for All, free college, higher taxes on the wealthy, or climate investment does not automatically translate into votes for every candidate carrying those policies. Election outcomes also cannot, by themselves, validate a historical-cycle theory. Democrats need a material program, but numerology about 40- and 80-year intervals is not a substitute for organizing, governing, or counting votes.

The crash framing misdirects

The headline converts a political argument into a prophecy the reporting cannot support. Turchin’s sequence—popular impoverishment, excess elite competition, and state breakdown—is presented as a warning model, not a demonstrated forecast of the next economic event. Howe’s generational framework is likewise an interpretation of history, not proof that the United States is scheduled for collapse.

That distinction matters because inevitability can conceal agency. Crashes do not arrive because a historical clock strikes midnight. Legislators choose fiscal policy. Regulators permit or constrain risk. Employers suppress or accept unionization. Courts expand or limit the political reach of money. Party officials decide whose interests receive protection.

The article also assigns vast historical upheavals to concentrated wealth with more certainty than its evidence here can carry. Economic inequality can intensify instability, but revolutions, civil wars, and democratic erosion have distinct causes and institutional histories. A forceful class analysis becomes less persuasive when analogy is made to do the work of proof.

The real warning

The consequential pattern is not that history mechanically repeats every eight decades. It is that concentrated wealth can purchase political access, weaken countervailing institutions, and redirect government toward asset holders while insecurity spreads below them. The article attributes that trajectory to Reagan-era policies continued across administrations: weaker unions, lower taxes on the wealthy, global labor arbitrage, and reduced public provision.

That account identifies a genuine political mechanism within the story’s own evidence. Economic pain erodes confidence when people repeatedly encounter institutions that protect wealth more reliably than wages, housing, healthcare, or food assistance. Demagogic politics can then redirect justified anger toward convenient targets while preserving the arrangements that produced the anger.

The danger of the crash metaphor is that it makes a chain of decisions sound like fate. The more precise conclusion is harsher: powerful people built the conditions AlterNet fears, public officials enabled them, and Democratic leaders still must decide whether to dismantle that structure or manage its decline. History offers no automatic progressive renewal. Institutions change when organized power forces the people controlling them to choose differently.

item.title: Trump voters turn to prayer after Republican rout
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, citing New York Times reporting, says Republicans lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress while Democrats swept every statewide race in Texas, including the governorship and a U.S. Senate seat. At a post-election Bible study in Pampa, a group of conservative men responded with mourning, anxiety and prayer. The men predicted higher taxes and attacks on farming, hunting and President Trump, though the account provides no policy evidence for those forecasts. Some
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, citing New York Times reporting, says Republicans lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress while Democrats swept every statewide race in Texas, including the governorship and a U.S. Senate seat. At a post-election Bible study in Pampa, a group of conservative men responded with mourning, anxiety and prayer.

The men predicted higher taxes and attacks on farming, hunting and President Trump, though the account provides no policy evidence for those forecasts. Some blamed newcomers from Democratic-leaning states, even as one participant acknowledged that Texas has elected Democrats before and another urged the group to hope the incoming officials would improve the country.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The supplied report does not provide the election date, complete results or independent confirmation of its sweeping electoral claims. Those omissions limit what can responsibly be concluded beyond AlterNet’s account of the gathering and its participants’ remarks.

Power changed hands

The men in Pampa are not the institutional actors in this story. The consequential power belongs to the officials who won the reported elections and, once seated, could control legislation, budgets, appointments and oversight. Voters produced the change; elected Democrats would exercise it.

Republican incumbents and candidates lost that authority according to the report. Yet the coverage spends little time on their records, decisions or failures. It substitutes the emotional reaction of loyal voters for an examination of why officeholders were rejected.

That is a familiar political dodge. When a governing party loses, portraits of bewildered supporters can turn an accountability event into a cultural tragedy. The defeated politicians recede from view while their voters become the story’s wounded protagonists.

Fear without a policy

The men’s predictions are expansive: war on farming, war on hunting, higher taxes, attacks on Trump. The reporting establishes these as fears, not as announced policies or demonstrated consequences. Calling every disfavored regulation or tax proposal a “war” does political work. It converts ordinary disputes over government into imagined persecution.

That framing also erases the interests Democrats reportedly campaigned on, including lower property taxes and protection for family farms. Those promises do not prove Democrats will deliver. They do show that the election cannot be explained simply as hostile outsiders imposing alien priorities on rural Texans.

The prayer group’s anxiety may be sincere. Sincerity does not make its premises accurate, and journalism should not confuse emotional intensity with evidence.

The outsider alibi

James Schaub blamed “transplants” who “don’t believe like we do,” despite the presence of Tom Hickey, who said he moved to Texas from the Pacific Northwest because it was conservative. The contradiction is instructive: migration is legitimate when it reinforces existing power and suspect when it threatens it.

The report also notes that Hispanic Texans now outnumber white Texans. That demographic fact does not establish how any group voted or why the reported sweep occurred. But paired with complaints about newcomers, it exposes a political reflex: when a durable majority stops winning, changing membership is treated as contamination rather than democracy functioning.

That rhetoric misdirects responsibility away from candidates who failed to assemble a majority. Voters are not trespassers in their own state because they reject the people who previously governed it.

Mourning is not dispossession

Losing an election is a loss of political control, not a loss of citizenship. Porter’s closing acknowledgment that Democrats are Americans is more revealing than it should be. It suggests that partisan identity had first placed their legitimacy in doubt.

The group remains free to worship, organize, criticize officials and vote again. Its members’ discomfort is real, but the article offers no evidence that their civil or political rights were taken from them. Treating electoral defeat as persecution inflates partisan disappointment into victimhood.

The larger pattern is a politics that regards conservative rule as the natural condition and any alternative as an invasion. That assumption shields defeated leaders from scrutiny and encourages supporters to explain rejection through cultural siege rather than governance. Power changed hands; the people accustomed to holding it were asked to recognize that they never owned it.

item.title: Even Trump doesn’t believe his own whoppers anymore
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s claim that impeachment would destroy Democrats was contradicted by Tuesday’s reported midterm results, which the outlet describes as a historic Democratic sweep across federal, state, and local offices. The article contends that the losses weakened Trump’s coalition and gave Democrats an opportunity to ask him to resign. The outlet reports that Trump denied responsibility for the defeat and focused publicly on White House ballroom construction. I
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s claim that impeachment would destroy Democrats was contradicted by Tuesday’s reported midterm results, which the outlet describes as a historic Democratic sweep across federal, state, and local offices. The article contends that the losses weakened Trump’s coalition and gave Democrats an opportunity to ask him to resign.

The outlet reports that Trump denied responsibility for the defeat and focused publicly on White House ballroom construction. It also says he replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, an elevation AlterNet interprets as a decision to intensify the deportation agenda despite reported voter opposition, including an AP finding that 68 percent of Hispanic voters disapproved of Trump’s deportation policies.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

AlterNet does not establish that Trump privately disbelieved his own statements. That is the author’s inference. The concrete story is simpler: after a sweeping electoral rejection, Trump publicly denied the scale of the rebuke and promoted Miller rather than changing course.

Power did not misunderstand the result

Trump held the presidency and the authority to choose his senior advisers. Republican senators retained the power to defend him, abandon him, or press him to leave. Democrats, strengthened by the reported election results, gained political leverage but not the unilateral power to remove a president outside the constitutional process.

That distinction matters. This was not a story about Trump failing to receive the electorate’s message. The reported appointment of Miller was an affirmative personnel decision. Whatever Trump believed privately, he used institutional power to preserve the political program voters had allegedly punished.

The lie is less important than the machinery

The article spends too much time speculating about whether Trump believed his boasts. A president’s sincerity is not the decisive question. Power operates through appointments, enforcement priorities, party discipline, and the willingness of other officials to cooperate.

AlterNet describes Miller as responsible for an immigration-enforcement system that harassed and terrorized immigrants and citizens, and it alleges killings by that system. Those are the outlet’s characterizations, not independently established findings in the supplied reporting. But the political point supported by the article is clear: Trump answered electoral losses tied partly to deportation policy by elevating the official most closely associated with that policy.

Calling this delusion risks turning agency into pathology. Denial can also function as propaganda: erase the defeat, reject accountability, and tell allies that no correction is required.

Republicans are not hostages

The article casts Trump as willing to destroy his party rather than permit a successor. But Republican officials are not powerless passengers on his “sinking ship.” They can defend him, confront him, or seek his resignation. Each option is a choice made by people with offices, votes, and constituencies.

The suggestion that Republicans might prefer a voluntary departure exposes their actual concern: controlling the political cost. They would not suddenly be rejecting the conduct described by AlterNet; they would be deciding that continued association had become electorally expensive. That is damage management, not accountability.

Democrats’ leverage has limits

Asking Trump to resign could force Republican officials to state publicly whether they still support him. It could also exploit tensions involving Vice President JD Vance, whom the article says blamed Trump’s war for the midterm losses. But a resignation demand is not costless simply because it requires no formal vote. It can become empty theater if Democrats substitute a press strategy for the harder work of investigation, legislation, oversight, or impeachment.

The electorate described by AlterNet gave Democrats leverage. Whether they convert it into institutional action is their decision. “Going on offense” means little unless it changes who exercises power, restrains abusive policy, or imposes consequences on those who enabled it.

The system rewards denial until it does not

The larger pattern is not that one politician stopped believing his own lies. It is that a political system can reward denial for years when a party, its officeholders, and its enforcement apparatus continue turning rhetoric into policy.

Election losses may weaken that arrangement, but they do not dismantle it automatically. If Miller’s reported elevation represented continuity after repudiation, then the response from Congress and the Republican Party determines whether the repudiation matters. Votes create an opening. Institutions—and the officials controlling them—decide whether power actually changes course.
